quote: The general explanation was that the Enron stock backstopping the Raptor hedge had declined in value such that Raptor would have a shortfall and would be unable to fully cover the hedge price that it owed to Enron.
context: Watkins testifies about the mechanism by which Enron's stock value was used operationally through normal financial reporting channels.

label: Raptor transactions presented to Board at high level
original_label: Raptor transactions presented to Board at high level
quote: He was aware that these Raptor transactions had been presented to the Board, but I said my understanding of the way these things are generally presented, it is high level summaries, and I am not so certain that the true nature was fully disclosed.
context: Watkins testifies to Lay that the Board saw sanitized presentations that obscured the true economic structure.

label: Related party footnote made $500 million appear net zero impact
original_label: Related party footnote made $500 million appear net zero impact
quote: I think that tended to make readers think that it was a $500 million gain offset by a $500 million loss. Therefore, zero impact on the income statement. However, without the Raptor transactions, Enron would have had a $500 million loss not covered by any gains running through the 2000 income statement.
context: Watkins testifies about how footnote disclosure created false impression of offsetting gains and losses masking actual losses.

label: Enron transaction accountants helped structure and convince Andersen
original_label: Enron transaction accountants helped structure and convince Andersen
quote: It is my opinion that Enron transaction accountants, most notably Ben Glisan, helped come up with the structure and come up with the support for the structure, and then convinced Andersen that it worked.
context: Watkins testifies to Congressman Deutsch that internal accountants created technical documentation to give legitimacy to the fraudulent structures.

label: V&E investigation scoped to avoid examination of accounting treatment
original_label: V&E investigation scoped to avoid examination of accounting treatment
quote: I was not aware that the investigation was being limited. I met with Vinson & Elkins on September 10 for roughly 3 hours and had no indication that it was a limited investigation. I only discovered that it was limited when I read their October 15 response, which was not provided to me.
context: Watkins testifies that V&E's investigation appeared thorough but was actually constrained to provide appearance of legitimacy without substance.

label: Causey and Lay falsely stated Raptors had no impact on 2000 earnings
original_label: Causey and Lay falsely stated Raptors had no impact on 2000 earnings
quote: An analyst asked the question, Okay. Enron has unwound these Raptor transactions. You have written off the transactions in the third quarter of 2001. If they had never existed at all, what would have been the income statement impact for the year 2000? And Mr. Causey responded that there would have been little or no impact, because we could have done these transactions elsewhere.
context: Watkins testifies that in a public investor call, executives made false statements to legitimize the structures and mask their true impact.

label: Document destruction to prevent evidence of repurchase rights
original_label: Document destruction to prevent evidence of repurchase rights
quote: My understanding was that Mr. Causey instructed our business unit that there could be nothing in writing that the business unit could buy it back, or Andersen would not let us have the sale treatment that we were getting in the funds flow statement.
context: Watkins testifies to Congressman Greenwood that evidence of the true economic arrangement was destroyed to maintain the appearance of legitimate sales.

label: Mark-to-market valuation based on subjective models
original_label: Mark-to-market valuation based on subjective models
quote: We do have some domestic assets that are fair value that are marked to a model that is somewhat subjective.
context: Watkins testifies to Congressman Markey about the use of subjective valuation models that provided legitimate appearance to inflated asset values.

label: Fastow coerced banks to invest in LJM through threat of losing business
original_label: Fastow coerced banks to invest in LJM through threat of losing business
quote: I had heard from friends that worked at Chase and Credit Suisse and Bank of America that Mr. Fastow was almost somewhat threatening, that if you didn't invest in LJM, Enron would not use you as a banker or an investment banker again. That he was threatening the institutions, that to get Enron business they should invest in LJM.
context: Watkins testifies to Chairman Greenwood about how legitimate business relationships were used to coerce participation in LJM schemes.

label: Skilling's August 14 resignation prompted Watkins' disclosure
original_label: Skilling's August 14 resignation prompted Watkins' disclosure
quote: On August 14, 2001, I was informed of Mr. Skilling's sudden resignation and felt compelled to inform Mr. Lay of the accounting problems that faced Enron.
context: Watkins testifies about the external event that broke the opportunity structure by removing a key offender and prompting her to act.

label: Powers Committee investigation contradicted Vinson & Elkins findings
original_label: Powers Committee investigation contradicted Vinson & Elkins findings
quote: Yet, until the Powers Report came out 2 weeks ago affirming her analysis of the Raptors, no one at Enron, or Andersen ever sought to address these concerns.
context: Chairman Greenwood describes in opening statement how independent investigation broke the opportunity structure by validating Watkins' claims.

label: October 16 equity writedown and earnings restatement forced disclosure
original_label: October 16 equity writedown and earnings restatement forced disclosure
quote: On October 16, Enron announced that, due to accounting errors and restructuring related to transactions involving LJM2, it was revising its shareholder equity numbers downward by $1.2 billion and posting a third quarter loss in excess of $500 million.
context: Congressman Stupak recounts the events when Enron's concealment broke down and the company was forced to publicly acknowledge the Raptor problems.

label: Watkins consulted Hecker who escalated through Andersen management
original_label: Watkins consulted Hecker who escalated through Andersen management
quote: Mr. Hecker indicated to me during our call that he hoped I wasn't right, because he didn't think their firm could stand another scandal following Waste Management and Sunbeam.
context: Watkins testifies about how consultation with an internal Andersen contact activated an external guardian that escalated concerns through firm hierarchy.

label: Watkins warned Lay of likelihood of discovery by disgruntled employees
original_label: Watkins warned Lay of likelihood of discovery by disgruntled employees
quote: We are under too much scrutiny, and there are probably one or two disgruntled pre-deployed employees who know enough about the funny accounting to get us into trouble.
context: Watkins testifies about her August memo to Lay predicting that external parties would eventually discover the wrongdoing through other whistleblowers.

label: Boeing leadership shifts from engineering to profit focus
original_label: Boeing leadership shifts from engineering to profit focus
quote: Harry Stonecipher, the Chief Executive Officer (CEO) of McDonnell Douglas became the President and Chief Operating Officer of Boeing. In 2004 he told the Chicago Tribune: 'When people say I changed the culture of Boeing, that was the intent, so it's run like a business rather than a great engineering firm. It is a great engineering firm, but people invest in a company because they want to make money.' Those sentiments, according to many observers and current and former Boeing employees, infected the company. They point to that philosophy, which focused on financial benefit rather than technical solutions and innovation, as setting the stage for many of the issues that ultimately contributed to the crashes of the two 737 MAX aircraft.
context: Committee report summarizing cultural shift at Boeing that motivated cost-cutting decisions throughout the 737 MAX program.

label: Cost pressures drive 737 MAX design choices
original_label: Cost pressures drive 737 MAX design choices
quote: In 2011, the estimated cost of building a brand-new airplane hovered around $10 billion while the cost of re-engining the existing 737 NG to develop the new 737 MAX airplane was only about $3 billion, according to Richard Aboulafia with the aviation industry market analysis firm, the Teal Group. Multiple current and former Boeing employees who have contacted the Committee since our investigation began have relayed dismay at the path they believe Boeing has taken since its merger with McDonnell Douglas.
context: Committee report on Boeing's choice to re-engine rather than build new aircraft, driven by cost considerations.

label: Senior program officials emphasize schedule pressure visibly
original_label: Senior program officials emphasize schedule pressure visibly
quote: To emphasize the significance of the 737 MAX program's schedule to Boeing employees, the Committee learned that senior program officials kept a 'countdown clock' in their conference room. Keith Leverkuhn, the former Vice President and General Manager of the MAX program, described the clock as an 'excitement generator' for Boeing's staff. But he also acknowledged it was to remind staff about the MAX's schedule. 'One of the mantras that we had was the value of a day,' he said, 'and making sure that we were being prudent with our time, that we were being thorough, but yet, that there was a schedule that needed to be met.'
context: Committee staff interview with former 737 MAX General Manager documenting production schedule pressure.

label: Chief Project Engineer compensated for maintaining schedule
original_label: Chief Project Engineer compensated for maintaining schedule
quote: The Committee has learned that to thank him for keeping to the MAX's production schedule, Boeing gave Michael Teal, the former Chief Project Engineer on the 737 MAX program, restricted stock options after the airplane's first flight in 2016 to show its appreciation for his work.
context: Committee investigation finding that Chief Project Engineer received financial incentives for schedule adherence.

label: Senior Boeing officials approve MCAS redesign for performance
original_label: Senior Boeing officials approve MCAS redesign for performance
quote: In March 2016, the General Manager of Boeing's 737 MAX program, Keith Leverkuhn, and Michael Teal, the former Chief Project Engineer on the 737 MAX program, both approved a redesign of MCAS to increase its authority to move the aircraft's stabilizer at low speed, in order to address 'stall characteristics' requirements necessary for FAA certification.
context: Committee findings on 737 MAX leadership approval of MCAS redesign that later contributed to crashes.

label: Pilots depend on Boeing-provided training and manuals
original_label: Pilots depend on Boeing-provided training and manuals
quote: Boeing provided Lion Air with a Flight Crew Operations Manual (FCOM) for its 737-8 MAX aircraft dated August 16, 2018, one year after learning that the AOA Disagree alert was not functioning on most 737 MAX aircraft, including those operated by Lion Air. The FCOM explained how the AOA Disagree alert was intended to work and provided absolutely no indication that Boeing was fully aware that the AOA Disagree alert on the Lion Air 737 MAX aircraft was not operational. As a result, Lion Air pilots who referenced Boeing's FCOM would have falsely believed that the AOA Disagree alert was functioning properly and would reliably warn them of a malfunctioning AOA sensor. Boeing knowingly deceived these pilots and its customer airlines.
context: Committee investigation finding that pilots received misleading Boeing manuals that concealed known defects.

label: FAA certification process relies on Boeing-provided data
original_label: FAA certification process relies on Boeing-provided data
quote: Early in the process, Boeing included limited information in initial briefings to FAA on the MAX's flight control software, MCAS, which subsequently has been cited as a contributing or potentially contributing factor in both accidents. However, Boeing presented the software as a modification to the existing speed trim system that would only activate under certain limited conditions. As such, MCAS was not an area of emphasis in FAA's certification efforts and therefore did not receive a more detailed review or discussion between FAA engineers and Boeing.
context: Department of Transportation Office of Inspector General report on how Boeing shaped FAA's understanding of MCAS during certification.

label: Airlines and passengers depend on certified aircraft safety
original_label: Airlines and passengers depend on certified aircraft safety
quote: In 2011, facing a competitive threat from Airbus's new, more fuel efficient, single-aisle A320 aircraft, Boeing believed it did not have time to create a new plane from scratch. Instead, it opted to modify its existing 737 NG aircraft to make it more fuel efficient. To help accomplish this, Boeing installed, larger, more fuel efficient engines on this new 737 derivative airplane model dubbed the 737 MAX aircraft.
context: Committee narrative establishing that airlines and passengers would receive an aircraft modified rather than newly designed, making them dependent on certification integrity.

label: BASOO severely understaffed relative to Boeing ODA personnel
original_label: BASOO severely understaffed relative to Boeing ODA personnel
quote: In October 2019, the Joint Authorities Technical Review (JATR) commissioned by the FAA to review the 737 MAX certification process reported that the Seattle-based Boeing Aviation Safety Oversight Office (BASOO), under the AIR Systems Oversight Division, was comprised of 45 FAA employees, including 24 total engineers, only 6 of whom were senior engineers, who overseeing the 1,500 Boeing-designated ODA unit members, or authorized representatives.
context: JATR report quantifying severe staffing disparity between FAA oversight office and Boeing ODA delegated personnel.

label: FAA lacks sufficient expertise and capacity for technical oversight
original_label: FAA lacks sufficient expertise and capacity for technical oversight
quote: The allocated staffing levels of 24 BASOO engineers may not be sufficient to carry out the work associated with retained items and with the conduct of oversight duties. There may be a lack of capacity and depth of experience of BASOO engineering members to approve and make findings of compliance for retained items. Depending on the number of entry-level engineers in the BASOO, there could be an imbalance of working-level engineers in relation to the number of senior engineers reasonably expected to be required given the complexity of work by Boeing. The BASOO may not be sufficiently staffed to review all the Boeing programs (737, 747, 767, 777, and 787). There are two technical staff assigned per Boeing program. Some of the technical staff are new engineers with limited airworthiness experience.
context: JATR report findings on BASOO staffing deficiencies for effective oversight.

label: FAA survey reveals lack of safety resources
original_label: FAA survey reveals lack of safety resources
quote: Within AVS overall, 52 percent did not believe they had enough resources and manpower dedicated to safety, 49 percent believed that safety concerns/incidents will not be addressed so they don't report them, and 43 percent do not believe the FAA appropriately delegates certification activities to organizational and individual designees.
context: FAA Aviation Safety Organization safety culture survey showing employee perceptions of resource constraints.

label: FAA delegates extensive 737 MAX certification to Boeing ODA
original_label: FAA delegates extensive 737 MAX certification to Boeing ODA
quote: In the case of the 737 MAX, in 2013, the FAA originally delegated 28 of 87 tasks to Boeing. However, this number rose to 79 of 91 activities by November 2016, four months prior to final certification of the 737 MAX aircraft.
context: Committee investigation documenting progressive delegation of certification authority to Boeing ODA.

label: FAA delegates acceptance of certification plans to Boeing ODA
original_label: FAA delegates acceptance of certification plans to Boeing ODA
quote: The FAA initially delegated acceptance of approximately 40% of the B737 MAX project's certification plans to the Boeing ODA. Additional certification plans that were originally retained for acceptance by the FAA were later delegated to the Boeing ODA as the certification project progressed. While the JATR team did not conduct an exhaustive review of other ODAs, the team observed that delegating the acceptance of certification plans does not appear to be a widespread practice for the FAA.
context: JATR report on unusual extent of FAA delegation of certification plan acceptance to Boeing.

label: FAA delegates MCAS system safety analysis to Boeing
original_label: FAA delegates MCAS system safety analysis to Boeing
quote: The NTSB also noted that the second certification plan, the EDFCS CP, 'indicated that approval of the EDFCS System Safety Analysis would be retained by the FAA and would not be proposed to be delegated to the Boeing ODA. The FAA retained approval of the SSA until revision K, submitted in January 2017. At that time, the FAA stamped the revision as 'rejected' due to the need to correct some information and simultaneously delegated approval of the SSA once the final edits were complete.' The EDFCS System Safety Analysis was one of three deliverables within the certification plan that the NTSB found were directly related to MCAS. In March 2017, two months after this System Safety Analysis was delegated to Boeing, the 737 MAX achieved final FAA certification approval.
context: NTSB system safety report documenting that FAA delegated MCAS safety analysis approval to Boeing shortly before certification.

label: Boeing Authorized Representatives experience undue pressure
original_label: Boeing Authorized Representatives experience undue pressure
quote: In November 2016, an internal Boeing survey of its ARs, who are supposed to represent the interests of the FAA, conducted at the height of the 737 MAX's certification activities, and provided to the Committee from a whistleblower, found that 39 percent of Boeing ARs that responded perceived 'undue pressure' and 29 percent were concerned about consequences if they reported potential 'undue pressure.'
context: Committee findings on internal Boeing survey revealing pressure on FAA representatives during 737 MAX certification.

label: FAA management overrules technical experts on 737 MAX rudder cable
original_label: FAA management overrules technical experts on 737 MAX rudder cable
quote: Despite that, three decades after the DC-10 crash, senior FAA management overruled both the professional judgement of a large group of FAA technical specialists and the recommendations of a safety review panel to permit the 737 MAX to be certified despite a design vulnerability that exposed the airplane's rudder cable to damage during an uncontained engine failure. Ultimately, the AIR manager responded that the deciding authority had considered the board's recommendations but determined that all rules, orders, and procedures had been followed with regards to the airplane's certification. This effectively closed the issue with FAA finding that the airplane was compliant with the requirement to minimize the risk of uncontained engine failure, despite the fact that a group of at least 18 FAA officials, including 13 FAA technical experts, four FAA managers and one FAA pilot had all recommended otherwise.
context: Committee finding on FAA management overruling 18 FAA experts' safety recommendations on 737 MAX.

label: FAA reverses safety decision after Boeing appeal
original_label: FAA reverses safety decision after Boeing appeal
quote: On February 22, 2019, FAA's BASOO formally rejected Boeing's design change based on experts' concerns that removing the copper foil on the wings created a greater risk of fuel tank ignition. However, Boeing appealed this decision. Exactly one week later, on March 1, 2019, FAA management overturned the BASOO's decision and allowed Boeing to continue producing the 787 Dreamliner without the copper foil to the dismay of FAA's technical experts.
context: Committee investigation on FAA management reversal of technical safety decision on 787 Dreamliner lightning protection.

label: FAA employees report industry pressure undermines safety culture
original_label: FAA employees report industry pressure undermines safety culture
quote: Many believe that AVS senior leaders are overly concerned with achieving the business-oriented outcomes of industry stakeholders and are not held accountable for safety-related decisions. Employees and managers reported that external pressure from industry is strong and is impacting the AVS safety culture. They [industry] just keep going up the chain until they get the answers they want. It feels like we are showing up to a knife fight with Nerf weapons. It is a challenge to be an equal match with Boeing in the meetings/conversations.
context: FAA Aviation Safety Organization safety culture survey with anonymous employee complaints about industry influence.

label: FAA reduces enforcement actions against Boeing
original_label: FAA reduces enforcement actions against Boeing
quote: In June 2015, FAA announced a new enforcement policy with a more collaborative and problem-solving approach called the Compliance Program. As a result of this change, FAA has increasingly used compliance actions, such as counseling or training, rather than enforcement actions, such as civil penalties, to address violations of safety standards. The Government Accountability Office (GAO) recently investigated the changes to these policies and their implications for FAA oversight. The GAO released their evaluation in August 2020 and reported a 90 percent decrease in the number of enforcement actions undertaken by the FAA's Aircraft Certification Office from 2012 to 2019.
context: GAO report documenting 90 percent decline in FAA enforcement actions coinciding with Boeing 737 MAX certification period.

label: Boeing engineer raises MCAS single sensor vulnerability
original_label: Boeing engineer raises MCAS single sensor vulnerability
quote: In 2015, a Boeing AR raised the question of whether MCAS was 'vulnerable to single AOA sensor failures....' Despite this, the aircraft was delivered with MCAS dependent on a single AOA sensor. Boeing's decision to allow MCAS to operate off of a single AOA sensor has been roundly criticized by a wide range of aviation safety experts.
context: Committee findings that Boeing engineer internal controls failed to prevent single-sensor MCAS vulnerability.

label: Boeing engineer raises concerns about repetitive MCAS activation
original_label: Boeing engineer raises concerns about repetitive MCAS activation
quote: In June 2016, a Boeing AR raised concerns following a test flight of the 737 MAX during which MCAS countered the pilot's attempts to trim the airplane, including concerns related to the vulnerability caused by faulty AOA readings. These concerns were discounted by the AR's Boeing colleagues, particularly Boeing's test pilots. However, faulty AOA data that resulted in uncommanded MCAS activation was a significant contributing factor in the crashes of both the Lion Air and Ethiopian Airlines flights.
context: Committee findings showing internal Boeing controls failed to escalate engineer concerns about repetitive MCAS.

label: Chief Project Engineer unaware of critical MCAS design aspects
original_label: Chief Project Engineer unaware of critical MCAS design aspects
quote: In a transcribed interview with Committee staff, Michael Teal, the former Chief Project Engineer on the 737 MAX program, acknowledged that when he approved the MCAS redesign in March 2016 he was unaware: 1) that MCAS operated from a single AOA sensor, 2) that MCAS could activate repeatedly, or 3) that Boeing had internal test data showing that one of its own test pilots took more than 10 seconds to react to uncommanded MCAS activation in a flight simulator, and described the results as 'catastrophic.'
context: Committee staff interview with Chief Project Engineer revealing lack of internal control over system design approval.

label: Boeing plant supervisor warns of production safety concerns
original_label: Boeing plant supervisor warns of production safety concerns
quote: In June 2018, Ed Pierson, a senior Boeing plant supervisor at the company's Renton, Washington 737 MAX production factory, emailed Scott Campbell, the 737 General Manager, requesting a meeting about 'safety concerns.' Mr. Pierson described multiple concerns about production and schedule pressures that were impacting quality control and safety issues. 'As a retired Naval Officer and former Squadron Commanding Officer,' wrote Pierson, 'I know how dangerous even the smallest of defects can be to the safety of an airplane. Frankly right now all my internal warning bells are going off. And for the first time in my life, I'm sorry to say that I'm hesitant about putting my family on a Boeing airplane.'
context: Committee investigation finding that internal Boeing controls flagged safety concerns to management.

label: Management response to plant supervisor safety concerns
original_label: Management response to plant supervisor safety concerns
quote: In July 2018, five weeks after Mr. Pierson's email, he finally met with Mr. Campbell in Mr. Campbell's office. According to Mr. Pierson's testimony to the Committee, he told Mr. Campbell that in the military they would temporarily halt production if they had the kinds of safety problems that Mr. Pierson was seeing on the MAX factory floor. Mr. Campbell allegedly responded: 'The military is not a profit-making organization.' Rather than heeding Mr. Pierson's dire warnings and thoroughly evaluating his safety concerns, Boeing continued to ramp up production on the 737 MAX and rehired retired Boeing employees to keep the production lines moving at the Renton plant.
context: Committee testimony on how Boeing management dismissed plant supervisor's safety warnings.

label: Boeing Authorized Representative approves MCAS downplaying strategy
original_label: Boeing Authorized Representative approves MCAS downplaying strategy
quote: The Boeing employees that devised the MCAS strategy were also making sure that their technical familiarity presentation to the European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) 'is consistent with the intent that MCAS is an addition to Speed Trim.' The Boeing AR concurred with Boeing's plan regarding its description of MCAS. As stated in the summary of the meeting, 'This will allow us to maintain the MCAS nomenclature while not driving additional work due to training impacts and maintenance manual expansions.'
context: Committee findings that Boeing's internal control (AR) approved strategy to downplay MCAS to regulators.

category: Legitimate access and separation from victims
label: Boeing employees access certification documents and processes
original_label: Boeing employees access certification documents and processes
quote: Individuals granted this specific designee authority are referred to throughout this report as authorized representatives or ARs. Civil aviation authorities worldwide—not just the FAA—administer delegation programs to leverage the product-specific knowledge of manufacturers' qualified employees to determine a product's compliance with government regulations. The FAA has relied on delegation authority for more than 50 years.
context: Committee explanation of how Boeing employees gained legitimate access to FAA certification authority.

label: Boeing describes MCAS as extension of speed trim to reduce scrutiny
original_label: Boeing describes MCAS as extension of speed trim to reduce scrutiny
quote: In May 2013, a group of Boeing employees working on the 737 MAX met to address another concern: 'If we emphasize MCAS is a new function there may be greater certification and training impact,' one Boeing employee wrote in a June 7, 2013, email summarizing the minutes of that meeting. They agreed to run the strategy by an Authorized Representative (AR) in Boeing's Autoflight group 'to ensure this strategy is acceptable.' The Boeing AR concurred with Boeing's plan regarding its description of MCAS. The intent of this plan was clear. It was not to avoid confusion about MCAS by regulators or 737 MAX pilots. The purpose of characterizing MCAS as an addition to speed trim was to avoid 'greater certification and training impact.'
context: Committee investigation of Boeing's deliberate strategy to mischaracterize MCAS to regulators.

label: Boeing documents MCAS downplaying strategy in compliance database
original_label: Boeing documents MCAS downplaying strategy in compliance database
quote: Boeing's item tracking compliance system database, called ITRACS, that documented this decision suggested that 'cost' was also a factor in the plan to downplay MCAS and to describe it as merely an addition to the Speed Trim System. On May 21, 2013, as part of that strategy meeting, the issue was presented this way in Boeing's ITRACS database: Problem Statement: Every new buzzword represents a company and airline cost via changed manuals, changed training, changed maintenance manuals. Recommended Action: Investigate deletion of MCAS nomenclature and cover under the umbrella of 'revised speed trim'.
context: Committee findings on Boeing's official documentation of cost-driven MCAS concealment strategy.

label: Boeing removes MCAS references from pilot training materials
original_label: Boeing removes MCAS references from pilot training materials
quote: In March 2016, Boeing sought, and the FAA separately approved, the removal of any references to MCAS from Boeing's Flight Crew Operations Manual (FCOM). Hours after the approval for MCAS's redesign was granted, Boeing sought, and the FAA approved, the removal of references to MCAS from Boeing's Flight Crew Operations Manual (FCOM). As a result, 737 MAX pilots were precluded from knowing of the existence of MCAS and its potential effect on aircraft handling without pilot command.
context: Committee findings on Boeing's removal of MCAS information from pilot training coinciding with system redesign.

label: Boeing withholds test pilot reaction time data from FAA
original_label: Boeing withholds test pilot reaction time data from FAA
quote: In 2012, at the start of the 737 MAX program, it took a Boeing test pilot more than 10 seconds to respond to uncommanded MCAS activation in a flight simulator, which the pilot found to be 'catastrophic.' Boeing never shared this information with the FAA, its MAX customers, or MAX pilots. From 2015 to 2018, the information regarding the fact that Boeing's own test pilot took more than 10 seconds to respond to uncommanded MCAS activation in a flight simulator leading to potentially 'catastrophic' consequences was included in at least six separate internal Boeing Coordination Sheets on MCAS's requirements. This indicates Boeing's keen awareness of the importance of this information. The Committee has found no evidence that Boeing shared this information with the FAA, its customers, or 737 MAX pilots.
context: Committee investigation documenting Boeing's concealment of critical test data from regulators and pilots.

label: Boeing fails to disclose inoperable AOA Disagree alert
original_label: Boeing fails to disclose inoperable AOA Disagree alert
quote: Boeing has publicly blamed its software supplier for an issue that tied the AOA Disagree alert, which was supposed to be standard on all 737 MAX aircraft, to an optional AOA Indicator display, the result of which was to render the AOA Disagree alert inoperable on more than 80 percent of the MAX aircraft. However, the Committee has learned that in July 2015, Boeing tested this software and failed to detect the problem. In August 2017, five months after the 737 MAX was certified by the FAA and three months after it entered revenue service, Boeing issued a problem report to its supplier complaining that the 737 MAX's AOA Disagree alert was tied to the optional AOA Indicator and therefore was not functioning on the vast majority of the 737 MAX fleet worldwide. Yet Boeing had previously approved of the version of the software that tied the AOA Disagree alert to the optional AOA Indicator display in July 2015.
context: Committee findings on Boeing's concealment of known defective alert system from FAA and customers.

label: Boeing postpones AOA alert fix for commercial reasons
original_label: Boeing postpones AOA alert fix for commercial reasons
quote: Rather than immediately informing the FAA and Boeing customers about this issue when it was discovered in August 2017, and advising Boeing to fix the problem via a software update as soon as possible, a Boeing AR consented to Boeing's plan to postpone the software update until 2020, three years later, so it could be done in conjunction with the rollout of Boeing's planned 737 MAX-10 aircraft. Although Boeing prepared a 'Fleet Team Digest' to inform its customers about the inoperable AOA Disagree alert, Boeing never sent it, keeping Boeing's customers in the dark about the inoperable alert until after the Lion Air crash.
context: Committee investigation of Boeing's decision to conceal known defect and delay remedy for business reasons.

label: Boeing continues delivering aircraft with non-functional alert
original_label: Boeing continues delivering aircraft with non-functional alert
quote: By the time of the Lion Air crash, Boeing had knowingly delivered approximately 200 MAX aircraft to customers around the world with non-functioning AOA Disagree alerts. Boeing did not acknowledge that the AOA Disagree alerts on more than 80 percent of the 737 MAX fleet were inoperative until after the Lion Air crash in October 2018.
context: Committee findings documenting Boeing's delivery of defective aircraft while concealing defect.

label: FAA accepts Boeing's cost arguments for regulatory exceptions
original_label: FAA accepts Boeing's cost arguments for regulatory exceptions
quote: Boeing was well aware early on of the risk posed to the 737 MAX program if it was required to implement an EICAS on the MAX. In June 2012, a Boeing employee gave a presentation titled: '737 MAX Certification Basis Risk Review: EICAS.' The presentation defined the issue this way: 'Numerous crew alerts on the 737Max are new or revised and per changed product regulation are required to meet latest amendment level. Current 737 flight crew alerting methods won't comply with latest regulation.' The presentation went on to say that a 'compliant design would be similar to the 787 or 767 tanker and include' EICAS as well as other features. Significantly, the presentation noted: 'IF we had to comply outright with regulation: Considerable program cost and schedule risk,' it asserted, and 'significant impact' on pilot training requirements. The presentation also cited the FAA's regulation regarding flightcrew alerting requirements. In the end, the FAA accepted Boeing's argument about the impracticality and the economic expense of installing EICAS on the 737 MAX.
context: Committee findings showing Boeing justified regulatory exception based on cost considerations that FAA accepted.

label: Boeing claims MCAS compliance despite design violations
original_label: Boeing claims MCAS compliance despite design violations
quote: The operating parameters of the MCAS system eventually placed on the 737 MAX aircraft violated Boeing's own internal design requirements which demanded that MCAS 'not have any objectionable interaction with the piloting of the airplane' and 'not interfere with dive recovery,' which occurred in both 737 MAX crashes.
context: Committee findings that Boeing certified MCAS in violation of its own internal design requirements.

label: Lion Air crash immediately reveals MCAS as factor
original_label: Lion Air crash immediately reveals MCAS as factor
quote: On October 29, 2018, Lion Air flight 610 crashed 13 minutes after takeoff killing 189 people. MCAS is quickly determined to be a major factor in the crash. Faulty AOA data erroneously caused MCAS to repetitively activate more than 20 times as the pilots battled MCAS for control of the aircraft. These safety issues were identified by Boeing's engineers years before the Lion Air crash, but they were not appropriately addressed or dismissed.
context: Timeline showing that MCAS deficiencies identified during development were realized in Lion Air crash.

label: Ethiopian Airlines crash and worldwide grounding
original_label: Ethiopian Airlines crash and worldwide grounding
quote: Ethiopian Airlines flight 302 crashes six minutes after takeoff killing all 157 passengers and crew. The FAA is the last civil aviation authority to ground the 737 MAX on March 13, 2020, three days after the Ethiopian crash. The 737 MAX aircraft has been grounded worldwide ever since.
context: Timeline marking second crash that triggered worldwide grounding, ending opportunity for further undetected wrongdoing.

label: Committee investigation launches after Ethiopian crash
original_label: Committee investigation launches after Ethiopian crash
quote: In March 2019, within days of the crash of Ethiopian Airlines flight 302, the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure (Committee), under the leadership of Chair Peter A. DeFazio and Subcommittee on Aviation Chair Rick Larsen, launched an investigation into the design, development, and certification of the 737 MAX aircraft and related matters that led to these crashes. Since then, the Committee has held five hearings on issues related to the 737 MAX program; written 23 oversight letters, including 12 records request letters; received an estimated 600,000 pages of records from Boeing, the FAA, airlines, and others; and conducted two dozen official interviews with current Boeing and FAA employees and others.
context: Committee report explaining initiation of systematic investigation after Ethiopian crash.

label: FAA grounds 737 MAX after Ethiopian crash
original_label: FAA grounds 737 MAX after Ethiopian crash
quote: On March 13, 2019, the FAA grounded the 737 MAX three days after the Ethiopian Airlines crash, following similar actions taken by China, the EU, and Canada, among others. Despite optimistic predictions at the time—that a simple software fix for MCAS would allow the 737 MAX to return quickly to service—the aircraft has been grounded for 18 months, with even more, newly discovered safety issues emerging since.
context: Committee report marking convergence break when external guardians (international regulators, media) forced FAA action.

label: Joint Authorities Technical Review examines certification process
original_label: Joint Authorities Technical Review examines certification process
quote: The Joint Authorities Technical Review (JATR) panel, established by the FAA's Associate Administrator for Aviation Safety in June 2019 as a direct result of the MAX crashes, and comprised of technical representatives from the FAA, National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA), and civil aviation authorities from Australia, Brazil, Canada, China, Europe, Indonesia, Japan, Singapore, and the United Arab Emirates, issued its final report in October 2019.
context: External investigation initiated after crash that examined Boeing and FAA certification practices.

label: Whistleblowers provide documents to Committee
original_label: Whistleblowers provide documents to Committee
quote: In addition, the Committee's investigation has been informed by records and information provided by numerous whistleblowers who have contacted the Committee directly with their concerns.
context: Committee investigation benefited from insider disclosure of Boeing internal documents and communications.

label: Former FAA engineer testifies about management safety overrides
original_label: Former FAA engineer testifies about management safety overrides
quote: In testimony to the Committee in December 2019, G. Michael Collins, a former FAA engineer with three decades of experience at the agency, who had knowledge of the Dreamliner's battery issues, said that during the airplane's certification process, an FAA engineer had proposed the use of a steel container to enclose the lithium batteries and prevent an uncontrolled fire should the batteries ignite. However, Mr. Collins said FAA managers did not support the engineer's proposal and left the certification decision about the batteries' installation to be made by the Boeing ODA instead. It was only after the grounding of the Dreamliner as a result of the extremely dangerous battery fires that the FAA mandated use of a steel container vented to the outside of the airplane.
context: Former FAA employee testimony to Committee exposing pattern of management overruling technical safety recommendations.

label: Chief Project Engineer approves MCAS without understanding it
original_label: Chief Project Engineer approves MCAS without understanding it
quote: Michael Teal, Vice President, Chief Project Engineer and Deputy Program Manager of the 737 MAX program, approved the design of MCAS, despite being unaware of basic facts about the system. He was not aware that MCAS relied on a single sensor. He was not aware that MCAS could activate repeatedly, and he was not aware that it had taken Boeing's own test pilot more than 10 seconds to respond to an uncommanded MCAS activation in a flight simulator and the pilot described his experience as "catastrophic."
context: Committee staff findings about Boeing's Chief Project Engineer's lack of awareness when approving MCAS design.

label: Chief Technical Pilot minimizes training requirement concerns
original_label: Chief Technical Pilot minimizes training requirement concerns
quote: In September 2013, Mark Forkner, Boeing's 737 Chief Technical Pilot, prepared a presentation that listed "Flight Crew Difference training level no greater than level B from 737NG family" as one of the "Ground Rules" for the 737 MAX.
context: Committee investigation documents Mark Forkner's role in establishing Level B training as a program goal.

label: Senior managers install countdown clocks to emphasize schedule priority
original_label: Senior managers install countdown clocks to emphasize schedule priority
quote: To remind Boeing employees of how critical sticking to the program's schedule was, Boeing's management introduced "countdown clocks" into the MAX program, and they made certain that they were easy to spot. In a transcribed interview with Committee staff, the former Boeing Vice President and General Manager of the 737 MAX program, Keith Leverkuhn, explained that there were countdown clocks associated with two major 737 MAX milestones—one was "power on" (when the airplane is powered up for the first time in the factory). The second was "first flight," which occurred on January 30, 2016, as scores of Boeing employees watched and applauded as the 737 MAX took off for the first time.
context: Committee investigation reveals Keith Leverkuhn's role in implementing visual reminders of schedule pressure during MAX development.

label: Production managers reject safety shutdown recommendations
original_label: Production managers reject safety shutdown recommendations
quote: On Wednesday, July 18, 2018, Mr. Pierson met with Mr. Campbell in Mr. Campbell's office. Mr. Pierson described the meeting as tense. According to Mr. Pierson's testimony to the Committee in December 2019, when he walked into Mr. Campbell's office, Mr. Campbell asked him: "Why are you here?" Mr. Pierson reminded him about their email exchange and the safety issues he had raised. Mr. Pierson recalled telling Mr. Campbell: "In … military operations, if we have these kinds of indications of unstable safety type of things, we would stop." Mr. Pierson was attempting to highlight his previous recommendation that the Renton plant's production line should temporarily cease operation because of his significant safety concerns. Mr. Campbell responded: "The military is not a profit-making organization," according to Mr. Pierson.
context: Committee investigation documents Scott Campbell's rejection of Ed Pierson's recommendation to halt production due to safety concerns.

label: FAA certification process as suitable target
original_label: FAA certification process as suitable target
quote: The committee has learned that when the MAX completed its first flight in January 2016, Michael Teal, Boeing's Chief Project Engineer on the 737 MAX program, received restricted stock options from Boeing to show appreciation for his efforts on the MAX program. Boeing's focus on reducing costs and meeting the production schedule resulted in excluding some technologies that may have improved the safety of the 737 MAX, such as synthetic airspeed.
context: Committee analysis of how Boeing's incentive structure prioritized schedule and cost over safety considerations.

label: Pilots and airlines unaware of MCAS system
original_label: Pilots and airlines unaware of MCAS system
quote: The unions representing pilots at American Airlines and Southwest Airlines, both of which operate the 737 MAX, allege their members were not made aware of MCAS and the system's ability to command the 737 MAX into a dive until after the Lion Air crash. Captain Dan Carey, then-President of the Allied Pilots Association, which represents American Airlines pilots, testified before the Subcommittee on Aviation in June 2019 that, "[t]he huge error of omission was the fact that Boeing failed to disclose the existence of the MCAS system to the pilot community around the world."
context: Committee investigation documents that pilots and airlines were not informed of MCAS's existence or capabilities before crashes occurred.

label: FAA Seattle AEG raises simulator training concerns about MAX systems
original_label: FAA Seattle AEG raises simulator training concerns about MAX systems
quote: In a May 10, 2015, internal email concerning this issue, an official in the Seattle AEG that would determine pilot training requirements wrote that "[t]he B737MAX presents some very contentious issues between Boeing and the FAA that will likely heat-up as we approach rollout and evaluation of the aircraft." Further, this official said, "[w]e have reason to believe that Boeing's assessment of B Level training differences (Computer Based Training) between the MAX and NG will be insufficient." Attached to that email, the AEG official included a memorandum that outlined the AEG's concerns regarding the possible need for simulator training on the 737 MAX as a result of several planned systems that were to be included on the aircraft.
context: Committee investigation shows FAA's Seattle Aircraft Evaluation Group identified concerns about simulator training requirements that were not ultimately enforced.

label: Boeing conducted TARAM risk analysis predicting 15 fatal crashes
original_label: Boeing conducted TARAM risk analysis predicting 15 fatal crashes
quote: On December 3, 2018, less than one week after Boeing's meeting with the APA pilots, the FAA prepared a quantitative risk assessment, known as a Random Transport Airplane Risk Analysis (R-TARA), that was based on the TARAM method of analysis regarding the risk to the 737 MAX fleet from continued operations. The analysis was based on the assumption that only one out of 100 pilots would fail to react properly to uncommanded MCAS activation resulting in Stabilizer Trim Runaway. Nevertheless, the results of the TARAM analysis indicated that even with the FAA's Emergency AD, but without a fix to MCAS, there could be more than 15 fatal 737 MAX crashes over the estimated 30-year lifetime of the fleet, then estimated to be 4,800 aircraft, resulting in over 2,900 deaths.
context: Committee investigation reveals FAA conducted analysis predicting catastrophic outcomes but did not ground the aircraft immediately.

label: FAA delegates certification authority to Boeing through ODA program
original_label: FAA delegates certification authority to Boeing through ODA program
quote: In a transcribed interview with Committee staff, the former Boeing Vice President and General Manager of the 737 MAX program, Keith Leverkuhn, explained that there were countdown clocks associated with two major 737 MAX milestones. The "countdown clocks" were located in the conference room where the 737 MAX program's senior-most management held "business performance reviews," "technical review boards," and other meetings. That organizational structure seems to have both dampened internal oversight at Boeing and diminished accountability regarding Boeing's 737 MAX program, particularly among its most senior leaders.
context: Committee findings on how Boeing's organizational structure under ODA arrangement reduced internal and external oversight effectiveness.

label: Boeing Authorized Representatives experience undue pressure from company
original_label: Boeing Authorized Representatives experience undue pressure from company
quote: A Boeing internal survey conducted in November 2016 at the height of the 737 MAX's certification activities, and provided to the Committee from a whistleblower, highlighted a number of findings related to undue influence at Boeing. Over 520 Boeing ODA members participated in the survey. Alarmingly, the survey found that 39 percent of the Boeing ARs that responded believed they had experienced undue pressure, painting a disturbing picture of cultural issues at Boeing that can undermine safety and oversight. In addition, of those 39 percent, 80 percent had encountered more than one situation where they perceived potential undue pressure.
context: Committee analysis of Boeing's internal survey showing FAA designees experience undue pressure from Boeing management.

label: FAA safety survey shows external industry pressure undermines agency mission
original_label: FAA safety survey shows external industry pressure undermines agency mission
quote: A recent internal survey of FAA employees in the Aviation Safety Organization (AVS) conducted in November and December 2019, found that 54 percent of FAA employees in the Aircraft Certification Service (AIR)—a part of AVS—said the FAA does not appropriately delegate certification activities to external FAA designees. The survey found 43 percent of AVS-wide respondents felt the same way. In addition, 56 percent of AIR employees believed there was too much external influence on the agency and that it was having an impact on safety. Another 49 percent of all AVS-wide respondents said they believed "safety concerns/incidents" will not be addressed by the agency.
context: Committee analysis of FAA's own internal survey revealing industry capture and weakened safety culture within the agency.

label: FAA removes MCAS reference from Emergency Airworthiness Directive
original_label: FAA removes MCAS reference from Emergency Airworthiness Directive
quote: At the last minute, an F.A.A. manager told agency engineers to remove the only mention of the system, according to internal agency documents and two people with knowledge of the matter," the New York Times reported. Mr. Dickson acknowledged this in response to QFRs from Chair DeFazio from the Committee's December 11, 2019, 737 MAX hearing. Suggesting that reference to MCAS would confuse pilots, the FAA Administrator wrote: "The FAA therefore decided to remove the MCAS reference from the draft AD so that flight crews would focus on runaway stabilizer recognition instead of attempting to troubleshoot MCAS."
context: Committee investigation reveals FAA deliberately removed MCAS reference from Emergency Airworthiness Directive after Lion Air crash.

label: FAA's BASOO finds Boeing compliance despite design defects
original_label: FAA's BASOO finds Boeing compliance despite design defects
quote: The FAA's review of MCAS prior to the Ethiopian Airlines crash. In January 2019, the FAA's Boeing Aviation Safety Oversight Office (BASOO), based in Seattle, began compiling an after action review, "737-8 MAX Maneuvering Characteristics Augmentation System Oversight Report," to look back at Boeing's submissions to FAA on MCAS as well as the office's certification work on that system. The Committee found the results of this review troubling. The FAA's draft review of MCAS following the Lion Air crash found it to be fully compliant with FAA regulations. If MCAS was compliant, yet it made the 737 MAX unsafe, this points to fundamental problems in the FAA's certification process.
context: Committee analysis of FAA's post-crash review that found Boeing compliant despite fundamental design flaws.

label: FAA's Ali Bahrami unfamiliar with TARAM analysis predicting fatal crashes
original_label: FAA's Ali Bahrami unfamiliar with TARAM analysis predicting fatal crashes
quote: Although Mr. Bahrami said he was unfamiliar with the details of the TARAM analysis that predicted 15 more fatal MAX crashes over the lifetime of the MAX fleet, he said he believed FAA officials "used the [TARAM] process the right way." He also acknowledged that the Emergency AD and the focus on pilot responses was only an interim fix. "[T]he fundamental issue was the redesign of the MCAS system, which [was] going to happen via software change, which immediately started right after the first accident," said Mr. Bahrami.
context: Committee investigation reveals FAA's Associate Administrator for Aviation Safety was unfamiliar with critical risk analysis.

label: Boeing exploits Level B training certification path to avoid simulator requirement
original_label: Boeing exploits Level B training certification path to avoid simulator requirement
quote: In July 2014, more than two years before the FAA would complete its pilot training evaluations and flight testing to make a determination, Boeing boldly claimed in a press release that no simulator training would be required. As an indication of how unusual Boeing's statement was, a Rockwell Collins official emailed FAA in April 2015 to inquire if Boeing had some level of agreement from the FAA that would allow it to make this claim. The FAA had not, in fact, made any agreements with Boeing and, as noted above, would not establish its final position on MAX pilot training requirements for two more years.
context: Committee investigation shows Boeing claimed simulator training compliance years before FAA certification process was complete.

label: Boeing uses separate coordination sheets to document MCAS catastrophic failure scenario
original_label: Boeing uses separate coordination sheets to document MCAS catastrophic failure scenario
quote: Between 2015 and 2018 Boeing issued six separate coordination sheets on MCAS that referenced the "catastrophic" consequences of a greater than 10-second pilot response time. The language throughout the years in the Boeing coordination sheets remained virtually unchanged regarding the consequences of the 10-second pilot reaction time. It said: Stabilizer runaways to pilot reaction (item D) were performed. These failures were arrested by use of the aisle stand cutout switch when the pilot recognized and reacted to the runaway. A typical reaction time was observed to be approximately 4 seconds. A slow reaction time scenario (>10 seconds) found the failure to be catastrophic due to the inability to arrest the airplane overspeed.
context: Committee investigation documents Boeing's repeated documentation of MCAS failure scenario over multiple years without sharing with FAA.

label: Boeing engineers raise MCAS single sensor concern but it is dismissed
original_label: Boeing engineers raise MCAS single sensor concern but it is dismissed
quote: In June 2016, a Boeing Authorized Representative (AR) asked his colleagues: "What happens when we have faulty AOA or Mach number?" His colleague, a Boeing engineer, quickly assured him that this was not something to worry about. "As for faulty AOA and/or Mach number," his colleague responded, "… if they are faulty then MCAS shuts down immediately." That may have been the intent, but that did not happen on Lion Air flight 610.
context: Committee investigation reveals Boeing engineers raised critical concerns about MCAS that were not adequately resolved.

label: Boeing engineer questions repetitive MCAS activation but concern dismissed
original_label: Boeing engineer questions repetitive MCAS activation but concern dismissed
quote: The following day, on June 16, 2016, another issue that would ultimately prove critical to the Lion Air crash was also raised by a Boeing employee. A different Boeing engineer who was aware of a Boeing test pilot having trouble countering repetitive MCAS activations during a test flight asked his colleague if the difficulties the Boeing test pilot had countering repetitive MCAS activation was a safety or a certification issue. His Boeing colleague responded: I don't think this is safety other then (sic) the pilot could fight the MCAS input and over time find themselves in a large mistrim. Unfortunately, that is exactly what happened in the Lion Air crash.
context: Committee investigation documents Boeing engineer raising concern about repetitive MCAS that was discounted.

label: Ed Pierson raises production safety concerns with Boeing management
original_label: Ed Pierson raises production safety concerns with Boeing management
quote: On Saturday, June 9, 2018, at 1:32 p.m., Mr. Pierson wrote an email to Scott Campbell, the General Manager of the 737 program and the senior most official at the Renton production facility. "Scott, I have some safety concerns that I need to share with you as the leader of the 737 Program," wrote Mr. Pierson. "Today we have 38 unfinished airplanes located outside the factory. My first concern is that our workforce is exhausted. …. Fatigued employees make mistakes," he warned. "My second concern is schedule pressure (combined with fatigue) is creating a culture where employees are either deliberately or unconsciously circumventing established processes."
context: Committee documents Ed Pierson's warning to Boeing production management about safety and quality issues due to schedule pressure.

label: Boeing General Manager dismisses production halt recommendation
original_label: Boeing General Manager dismisses production halt recommendation
quote: Mr. Campbell responded to Mr. Pierson at 6:48 a.m. the following morning, Sunday, June 10, 2018. His reply suggested he clearly understood Mr. Pierson's concerns. Mr. Campbell wrote: We need and will remind everyone constantly that quality is number one and schedule come [sic] after that. However, it took more than five weeks and another email from Mr. Pierson to Mr. Campbell's assistant to arrange a meeting on the topic.
context: Committee investigation shows Boeing management's weak response to safety concerns raised by production supervisor.

label: Production continued despite engineer warnings about process quality
original_label: Production continued despite engineer warnings about process quality
quote: Rather than heeding Mr. Pierson's dire warnings and thoroughly evaluating his safety concerns, Boeing continued to ramp up production on the 737 MAX. Lion Air flight 610 crashed three months later. One week after Mr. Pierson and Mr. Campbell met, Boeing held its second quarter 2018 quarterly earnings call with reporters and industry analysts. Boeing's then-CEO Dennis Muilenburg noted that production on the 737 MAX was continuing to ramp up and that the company had delivered 162 MAX aircraft to its customers to date.
context: Committee investigation reveals Boeing ignored internal warnings and continued production expansion.

category: Legitimate access and separation from victims
label: Boeing uses certification submission process to conceal MCAS information
original_label: Boeing uses certification submission process to conceal MCAS information
quote: In March 2014, a senior Boeing employee expressed concern that adding new "Asymmetry and Authority alerts" to the 737 MAX could potentially endanger Level B computer-based training requirements. "We told all our customers MAX will only require up to Level B training," wrote the Boeing employee. The employee was clearly concerned about the impact increased training requirements could have. "This would have very severe consequences for the MAX program," the employee wrote to Boeing colleagues more than two years before the FAA made a decision regarding pilot training requirements.
context: Committee analysis showing Boeing used normal certification process to manage information about training implications.

category: Legitimate access and separation from victims
label: Mark Forkner requests removal of MCAS from pilot training materials
original_label: Mark Forkner requests removal of MCAS from pilot training materials
quote: The redesign of MCAS, which was approved in March 2016, also coincided with Boeing's efforts to remove MCAS from pilot training materials for its MAX customers. In a March 30, 2016, email, Mr. Forkner assured an FAA official that references to MCAS could be deleted from the official FCOM and other 737 MAX training documents because MCAS is "completely transparent to the flight crew and only operates WAY outside of the normal operating envelope." The FAA ultimately permitted Boeing to remove references to MCAS.
context: Committee investigation documents Boeing's use of normal certification process to remove MCAS references from required pilot training materials.

category: Legitimate access and separation from victims
label: Boeing supplies FCOMs to airlines depicting non-functional AOA Disagree alert
original_label: Boeing supplies FCOMs to airlines depicting non-functional AOA Disagree alert
quote: Boeing provided a Flight Crew Operations Manual (FCOM) on the 737 MAX to P.T. Lion Mentari, the parent company of Lion Air, dated August 16, 2018, a full year after Boeing first learned that the AOA Disagree alert was not working on most 737 MAX aircraft. Yet the FCOM still contained a description of a functioning AOA Disagree alert. Specifically, the FCOM Boeing delivered to Lion Air continued to show pilots an image of a functioning AOA Disagree alert, and assured them that the alert, "Indicates the Captain's (left) and First Officer's (right) angle of attack values disagree by more than 10 degrees for more than 10 continuous seconds."
context: Committee investigation reveals Boeing provided manuals to airlines describing non-functional safety features as operational.

label: Boeing describes MCAS as routine in February 2015 presentation
original_label: Boeing describes MCAS as routine in February 2015 presentation
quote: In July 2014, before efforts to remove that material took place, Mark Forkner, the 737 Chief Technical Pilot at Boeing, and a colleague, gave a 75-page presentation to Southwest Airlines that was labeled: "737-8 MAX Flight Crew Training (For Southwest Airlines internal use only)." Two slides gave a description of MCAS describing its purpose and operating envelope. Among other things, the slides explained that MCAS "[a]ugments pitch stability at high angles-of-attack," that it is "[r]equired to maintain compliance to FAA Certification requirements," that it "[o]perates outside of normal operating envelope," and that it is "[d]isabled with autopilot engaged."
context: Committee investigation shows Boeing provided limited technical MCAS information to Southwest Airlines in 2014 but did not disclose it to pilots.

label: Boeing omits MCAS from Emergency Operations Manual Bulletin after Lion Air crash
original_label: Boeing omits MCAS from Emergency Operations Manual Bulletin after Lion Air crash
quote: On November 6, 2018, eight days after the Lion Air crash, Boeing issued an Operations Manual Bulletin (OMB) that directed airline operators and flight crews to various flight crew procedures to address erroneous angle-of-attack (AOA) sensor data. The OMB issued by Boeing had the subject line, "Uncommanded Nose Down Stabilizer Trim Due to Erroneous Angle of Attack (AOA) During Manual Flight Only." Noticeably absent from the Boeing bulletin was any reference to the "Maneuvering Characteristics Augmentation System" or "MCAS." It did include a description of the operational conditions associated with MCAS, though.
context: Committee investigation documents Boeing's deliberate omission of MCAS system name from post-crash bulletins to pilots.

label: Boeing official describes MCAS as just software to minimize significance
original_label: Boeing official describes MCAS as just software to minimize significance
quote: On November 27, 2018, two weeks after Boeing issued its MOM alert to its 737 MAX customers, Boeing officials sat down with representatives from the Allied Pilots Association. According to the draft transcript of that meeting, one of the Boeing officials attempted to explain away MCAS to the American Airlines pilots: MCAS is a control law, which it's–it's in the flight control system. So it's just a little bit of software in the flight control system that is designed to change the handling characteristics of the airplane at high angles of attack.
context: Committee investigation reveals Boeing officials minimized MCAS significance in meeting with pilot union representatives.

label: Boeing claims pilot is redundant system component for MCAS
original_label: Boeing claims pilot is redundant system component for MCAS
quote: At the meeting with American Airline pilots, one of the Boeing officials said that despite the reports that MCAS was a "single-point failure" system, that was not true because they believed the pilots were part of the "system" and essentially served as a backup to any technical failure of MCAS. "So the [MCAS] function and trained pilot are part of the system," said one of the Boeing officials. "So rightly or wrongly, that was the design criteria, and that's how they're being certified with the – the – the system and the pilot working together," he said.
context: Committee investigation documents Boeing's argument that pilots served as fail-safe for MCAS design.

label: Boeing presents MCAS design changes as compliant with all regulations
original_label: Boeing presents MCAS design changes as compliant with all regulations
quote: Boeing's MCAS overview made this point absolutely clear. The presentation identified multiple missteps, yet Boeing concluded none of these resulted in any process violations or non-compliances with the FAA's regulations. For instance, Boeing concluded: Erroneous AOA data was "identified and not analyzed as part of" the single & multiple failure assessment "per Engineering judgment." The single & multiple failure assessment "analysis [was] complete prior to the design change to MCAS control law during flight test." However, "[r]eevaluation of [the] design change [was] not required…" There was "[n]o process violation or non-compliance" for the removal of the MCAS Control Law from the Flight Crew Operations Manual (FCOM) and the pilot Differences Training Table.
context: Committee investigation reveals Boeing's post-Lion Air presentation to FAA claiming design complied with all regulations despite multiple identified deficiencies.

label: Lion Air crash triggers investigation of MCAS and AOA Disagree alert issue
original_label: Lion Air crash triggers investigation of MCAS and AOA Disagree alert issue
quote: Following the October 29, 2018, Lion Air crash, in which erroneous AOA data appeared to be a contributing factor, Boeing finally briefed the FAA on the defective AOA Disagree alerts on MAX planes lacking optional AOA Indicators. Then, on November 6, 2018, Boeing issued an Operations Manual Bulletin (OMB), which cautioned pilots about the risk of uncommanded downward stabilizer trim due to erroneous AOA data, and noted that one of the indications that a MAX was experiencing erroneous AOA data was the "AOA DISAGREE alert (if the AOA indicator option is installed)." The following day, the FAA issued an Emergency Airworthiness Directive (AD) which offered a similar warning to MAX pilots.
context: Committee investigation documents how Lion Air crash led Boeing and FAA to finally disclose AOA Disagree alert defect to customers.

label: Media reports MCAS information after Boeing MOM disclosure
original_label: Media reports MCAS information after Boeing MOM disclosure
quote: Within 48 hours of releasing the MOM to Boeing's 737 MAX customers, U.S. and foreign media outlets quickly began reporting on the existence of the MCAS, its operational function and its role in the Lion Air crash. On November 12, 2018, the Seattle Times ran a story with the headline: "U.S. pilots flying 737 MAX weren't told about new automatic systems change linked to Lion Air crash." The next day the Wall Street Journal ran a story with the headline: "Boeing Withheld Information on 737 Model, According to Safety Experts and Others."
context: Committee investigation documents media detection and reporting of Boeing's failure to disclose MCAS to pilots.

label: FAA receives Boeing data on March 13 leading to MAX grounding
original_label: FAA receives Boeing data on March 13 leading to MAX grounding
quote: According to Mr. Bahrami, "Beth basically said, Ali, we have some information that we need to share with you…." Mr. Bahrami did not recall who was in the room with him, but Boeing sent them data that they put on a screen. They superimposed the traces from both the Lion Air flight and the Ethiopian Airlines flight on the screen and Boeing explained their similarities. They did not yet have the flight data recorder from the Ethiopian Airlines flight. Boeing also told Mr. Bahrami that they found physical evidence at the crash site. "The physical evidence they found was the flap actuator," said Mr. Bahrami. "[The f]lap actuator was in a retract position. And MCAS gets activated when flaps are up," said Mr. Bahrami. I saw that and I said, thank you, anything else? And they said, well, what are you going to do? I said, we'll get back to you. And I walk out of my office, went to Dan's [Dan Elwell, then-Acting FAA Administrator's] office, and I said, we need to ground the fleet.
context: Committee investigation documents Boeing's presentation of evidence about Ethiopian Airlines crash on March 13, 2019, leading to FAA decision to ground MAX fleet.

label: FAA issues Emergency Airworthiness Directive grounding MAX fleet
original_label: FAA issues Emergency Airworthiness Directive grounding MAX fleet
quote: At 3:00 p.m. on March 13, 2019, the FAA grounded the 737 MAX fleet. The FAA issued a brief statement that said: The FAA is ordering the temporary grounding of Boeing 737 MAX aircraft operated by U.S. airlines or in U.S. territory. The agency made this decision as a result of the data gathering process and new evidence collected at the site and analyzed today. This evidence, together with newly refined satellite data available to FAA this morning, led to this decision.
context: Committee documents FAA's emergency grounding order of 737 MAX fleet following Ethiopian Airlines crash evidence.

label: Manufacturing defects discovered during MAX grounding period
original_label: Manufacturing defects discovered during MAX grounding period
quote: From software glitches to manufacturing defects and production quality deficiencies, several areas of concern related to both previously identified and newly found problems have emerged following the 737 MAX's grounding in March 2019. These include: Nonconforming Slat Tracks. In December 2019 and January 2020, the FAA proposed $9.3 million in civil penalties against Boeing for the company's alleged installation of slat tracks that were weakened during the manufacturing process. Flight Control Computer. In January 2020, the two flight control computers installed on a 737 MAX test airplane failed to properly power-up after the installation of updated software. Wire Bundles. Electrical wiring originally installed on 737 MAX airplanes did not meet FAA regulations for safe wire separation.
context: Committee investigation documents new manufacturing and software defects discovered in MAX aircraft during 18-month grounding period.

label: FAA inspects fuel tank debris in MAX aircraft in storage
original_label: FAA inspects fuel tank debris in MAX aircraft in storage
quote: In February 2020, Boeing discovered that some of its stored 737 MAX airplanes had foreign object debris (FOD) such as rags and tools in their fuel tanks—a condition that creates a potential safety hazard. The presence of FOD that Boeing found in the fuel tanks and other interior spaces in approximately half of the estimated 400 undelivered 737 MAX airplanes that it inspected is a production quality control issue that Boeing has also experienced on other types of aircraft that it has manufactured. A weekly report by FAA's Seattle Aircraft Certification Office on May 11, 2020, contained an entry on "FOD in Fuel Tanks" on 737 MAX airplanes which noted that the FAA had received several messages from foreign civil aviation authorities, including the European Union Aviation Safety Agency, expressing concern for "Boeing Quality Issues."
context: Committee investigation documents discovery of foreign object debris in stored MAX aircraft and FAA correspondence with foreign regulators about quality issues.

label: Synthetic airspeed rejected by management due to cost and training implications
original_label: Synthetic airspeed rejected by management due to cost and training implications
quote: A Boeing employee involved in this issue recently wrote to the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation about his frustrations related to synthetic airspeed and other issues regarding the development of the 737 MAX. "I specifically advocated for a system that would have enabled" synthetic airspeed to be placed on the 737, "but upper management shut down the project over cost and training concerns," he wrote. The notion of adding synthetic airspeed to the MAX was raised three separate times with Boeing managers and rejected on the basis of cost and potential pilot training impacts, according to an internal Boeing complaint filed by a Boeing engineer.
context: Committee investigation documents Boeing engineer's complaint that management rejected safety feature due to cost and training concerns.

label: Technical pilot pressured to emphasize MAX similarity to NG in FAA briefing
original_label: Technical pilot pressured to emphasize MAX similarity to NG in FAA briefing
quote: Furthermore, in a May 2014 email to a Boeing colleague discussing an upcoming briefing to the FAA regarding pilot training issues, Mr. Forkner, wrote: "We definitely want to emphasize how similar the MAX will be to the NG with regards to handling characteristics/qualities, as opposed to different/changed."
context: Committee investigation reveals Boeing's Chief Technical Pilot directing messaging strategy to minimize training differences in FAA briefings.

label: Boeing technical pilot disparages foreign airlines questioning simulator training
original_label: Boeing technical pilot disparages foreign airlines questioning simulator training
quote: For example: In response to a March 2017 request from Boeing's Africa & Caribbean Sales Director related to an inquiry from a customer airline about costs to provide training to its flight crews, Mr. Forkner wrote: "I want to stress the importance of holding firm that there will not be any type of simulator training required to transition from the NG to the MAX. Boeing will not allow that to happen. We'll go face to face with any regulator who tries to make that a requirement." In June 2017, in response to an airline that was considering simulator-based training for its pilots transitioning to the MAX, Mr. Forkner wrote in an email, "There is absolutely no reason to require your pilots to require a MAX simulator to begin flying the MAX." In a separate instant message exchange with a Boeing colleague, also in June 2017, Mr. Forkner wrote: "Now friggin Lion Air might need a sim to fly the MAX, and maybe because of their own stupidity. I'm scrambling to figure out how to unscrew this now! idiots"
context: Committee investigation documents Boeing's Chief Technical Pilot using inappropriate language and aggressive tactics to discourage airlines from implementing simulator training.

label: Boeing technical pilot claims success in talking airlines out of simulator training
original_label: Boeing technical pilot claims success in talking airlines out of simulator training
quote: In December 2017, Mr. Forkner informed a colleague in an instant message exchange that he made a foreign airline "feel stupid about trying to require any additional training requirements." "… I just jedi mind tricked this [sic] fools," Mr. Forkner wrote. "I should be given $1000 every time I take one of these calls," he said, and then added "I save this company a sick amount of $$$$"
context: Committee investigation documents Boeing's Chief Technical Pilot boasting about persuading airlines to abandon simulator training requirements.

label: Boeing awards technical pilots for securing Level B training approval
original_label: Boeing awards technical pilots for securing Level B training approval
quote: In fact, the Committee has learned that in September 2016, one month after the FAA provided Boeing with provisional approval for Level B (non-simulator) training for 737 MAX pilots, Mr. Forkner and his team of technical pilots that had been promoting Level B training were granted an award for their efforts from Boeing. An internal Boeing email said that the technical pilot team received the company's Commercial Aviation Services (CAS) Service Excellence Award on September 14, 2016, "along with the Training Development Team for their role is [sic] developing the MAX Level B differences training which was approved by the FAA."
context: Committee investigation reveals Boeing rewarded team members responsible for securing Level B training approval.

label: Boeing employees raise concerns about MAX simulator quality and schedule pressure
original_label: Boeing employees raise concerns about MAX simulator quality and schedule pressure
