label: Boeing designed MCAS to address pitch characteristics
original_label: Boeing designed MCAS to address pitch characteristics
quote: During the preliminary design stage of the 737 MAX 8, Boeing tests and analysis revealed that the addition of the LEAP-1B engine and associated nacelle changes produced an Airplane nose-up pitching moment when the Airplane was operating at high angles of attack (AOA) and mid Mach numbers. This nose-up pitching moment was deemed likely to affect the stick force per g (FS/g) characteristics required by FAR 25.251, FAR 25.255, and the controllability and maneuverability requirements of FAR 25.143(f). After the study of various options for addressing this issue, Boeing implemented aerodynamic changes as well as a stability augmentation function called the Maneuvering Characteristics Augmentation System (MCAS), as an extension of the existing Speed Trim System (STS), to improve Airplane handling characteristics and improve static longitudinal stability at elevated angles of attack.
context: The investigation report describes Boeing's design decision to implement MCAS in response to discovered aerodynamic characteristics of the MAX design.

label: Flight crews lack detection and response capability
original_label: Flight crews lack detection and response capability
quote: AOA Monitoring: The ADIRU performed a limited monitoring of the AOA sensor, based on the signal received from the resolver. The ADIRU generates 'AOA signal failed' information if it detects one or more of the following conditions: the resolver output is zero volts; the combined amplitude is outside the acceptable range; The calculated AOA vane shaft angle is outside the range defined by the mechanical stops. The ADIRU generates 'AOA failed' information when it detects any of the above conditions or if the reference (excitation) voltage signal provided to the AOA sensor from the Airplane 28VAC power bus is out of range.
context: The investigation documents the limited monitoring of AOA sensors, showing that certain failure modes could produce erroneous values without alerting the crew.

label: Single AOA sensor can affect multiple safety-critical systems
original_label: Single AOA sensor can affect multiple safety-critical systems

context: The investigation analysis identifies that a single failed AOA sensor can cascade failures across multiple aircraft systems, making flight crews vulnerable.

original_label: FAA oversight limited by heavy workloads

label: FAA did not require direct involvement in MCAS
original_label: FAA did not require direct involvement in MCAS

Some key issues that will always require direct FAA involvement include rulemaking (such as for special conditions), development of issue papers, and compliance findings considered unusual or typically reserved for the FAA. While these items establish the minimum direct FAA involvement, additional critical safety findings must also be identified based on the safety impact or the complexity of the requirement or the method of compliance.
context: The investigation cites FAA guidance indicating that critical safety items require direct FAA involvement, suggesting the agency had discretion over the extent of its oversight of MCAS.

label: AOA DISAGREE alert depends on pilot selection of optional AOA display
original_label: AOA DISAGREE alert depends on pilot selection of optional AOA display
quote: AOA DISAGREE alert: As shown in (figure 12) the 'AOA DISAGREE' message appears on the Captain and First Officer PFD when the values of the left and right AOA transmitted by the ADIRUs differ by 10° or more for 10 continuous seconds. The annunciation is only displayed in the air because AOA values are unreliable when the Airplane is stationary on the ground. The AOA DISAGREE message was first implemented on the Boeing 737NG fleet in 2006 in response to customer requests. Since 2006, the AOA DISAGREE alert has been installed on all newly manufactured Boeing 737 NG Airplanes, and is available as a retrofit for older Airplanes. The AOA DISAGREE alert has not been considered as a safety feature by Boeing, and is not necessary to safely operate the Airplane.
context: The investigation documents that the AOA DISAGREE alert, which could have warned of the failed sensor, was not displayed on ET-302 because it was linked to an optional feature.

label: Boeing determined AOA DISAGREE not required until 2020 software upgrade
original_label: Boeing determined AOA DISAGREE not required until 2020 software upgrade
quote: In 2017, however, within several months after beginning Boeing 737- 8 (MAX) deliveries, Boeing identified that the Boeing 737-8 (MAX) display system software did not correctly implement the AOA DISAGREE alert requirements. As with the Boeing 737 NG, the Boeing display system requirements for the Boeing 737-8 (MAX) called for the activation of the AOA DISAGREE alert as a standard feature on all Airplanes. The software delivered to Boeing, however, linked the AOA DISAGREE alert to the AOA position indicator, which is an optional feature on the Boeing 737 (MAX) series. Accordingly, the software activated the AOA DISAGREE alert only if an airline opted for the AOA indicator. At the time of the accident, Boeing advised that the AOA indicator had been selected by approximately 20% of airlines. When the discrepancy between the AOA display requirements and the software was identified, Boeing determined that the absence of the AOA DISAGREE alert did not adversely impact Airplane safety, certification or operation. Accordingly, Boeing concluded that the existing functionality was acceptable until the originally intended functionality could be implemented in a display system software upgrade scheduled for the third quarter of 2020.
context: The investigation documents Boeing's decision to delay implementation of a critical alert, scheduling a fix only for 2020 rather than issuing an immediate retrofit.

label: Boeing FHA assumptions did not address erroneous AOA cascades
original_label: Boeing FHA assumptions did not address erroneous AOA cascades
quote: The FHA evaluations were conducted by Boeing in their Engineering Cab using FAA guidance regarding pilot response to flight control failures requiring trim input that is contained in FAA Advisory Circular AC25.7C. In particular, Boeing uses the following assumptions in its flight controls FHAs: Uncommanded system inputs are readily recognizable and can be counteracted by overriding the failure by movement of the flight controls in the normal sense by the flight crew and do not require specific procedures. Action to counter the failure shall not require exceptional piloting skill or strength. The pilot will take immediate action to reduce or eliminate increased control forces by re-trimming or changing configuration or flight conditions. Trained flight crew memory procedures shall be followed to address and eliminate or mitigate the failure.
context: The investigation documents the assumptions Boeing used in its hazard assessment, showing they presumed pilot recognition and immediate action to counter MCAS failures.

label: Boeing FHA did not simulate erroneous AOA with MCAS activation
original_label: Boeing FHA did not simulate erroneous AOA with MCAS activation
quote: As originally delivered, the MCAS became active during manual (autopilot not engaged), flaps-up flight when the AOA value received by the master FCC exceeded a threshold based on Mach number. When activated, the MCAS provided a high rate automatic trim command to move the stabilizer towards Airplane Nose Down. Thus, the specific failure modes that could lead to uncommanded MCAS activation, such as an erroneous high AOA input to the MCAS, were not simulated as part of these functional hazard assessment validation tests. As a result, additional flight deck effects (such as IAS DISAGREE and ALT DISAGREE alerts and stick shaker activation) resulting from the same underlying failure (for example, erroneous AOA) were not simulated and were not documented in the stabilizer trim and autoflight safety assessment reports reviewed by the NTSB.
context: The investigation reveals that Boeing's hazard assessment for MCAS did not test the scenario that actually caused the accident—erroneous AOA triggering MCAS along with other cascading system failures.

label: Boeing FHA classified MCAS as Major not Catastrophic hazard
original_label: Boeing FHA classified MCAS as Major not Catastrophic hazard
quote: TABLE 28: RESULTS OF PRELIMINARY HAZARD ASSESSMENT FOR REVISED MCAS AUTHORITY: Hazard: Uncommanded MCAS function operation up to its maximum authority; Hazard classification: Major*; Uncommanded MCAS function operation equivalent to a 3 second mistrim: Major
context: The investigation documents Boeing's hazard classification of uncommanded MCAS activation as Major rather than Catastrophic, based on assumptions about pilot recognition and recovery.

label: Boeing assumed pilots could counter MCAS with column alone
original_label: Boeing assumed pilots could counter MCAS with column alone

Airplane can be returned to steady level flight using available column (elevator) alone or stabilizer trim. Continuous unintended nose down stabilizer trim inputs would be recognized as a Stab Trim or Stab Runaway failure and procedure for Stab Runaway would be followed.
context: The investigation documents Boeing's assumptions that uncommanded MCAS could be controlled with column alone, assumptions that were contradicted by the accident scenario.

label: Left AOA sensor failed during takeoff roll
original_label: Left AOA sensor failed during takeoff roll

Then after, the left AOA value reached 74.5° in ¾ seconds while the right AOA reached a Maximum value of 15.3°, the difference between the left and the right AOA values decreased from 59° to approximately 49° near the end of the recording, prior to the final dynamic behavior that was exhibited.

label: MCAS activated repeatedly despite crew trim inputs

label: Crew unable to manually trim with cutout switches engaged

label: Fourth MCAS activation after cutout switches restored

label: Functional Hazard Assessment did not test repetitive MCAS activations

label: FHA classified uncommanded MCAS as Major instead of Catastrophic

label: Boeing did not perform fault tree analysis for Major-classified MCAS
original_label: Boeing did not perform fault tree analysis for Major-classified MCAS

label: Ethiopian Airlines raised critical MCAS questions to Boeing
original_label: Ethiopian Airlines raised critical MCAS questions to Boeing
quote: First; According to the briefing there was no problem with the MCAS system at the time of the accident except being triggered at the wrong moment during the flight due to a single erroneous AOA data. Then why is the system designed in such a way that it operates depending on a single data source, especially when it is of a serious consequences, instead of interrogating data from other AOA sensors? Second; any average skilled pilot experiencing multiple failures, as it were, would react to the abnormalities depending on their sequence of urgency starting with a stick shaker. All simulator trainings, so far provided, require at the first activation of a stick shaker to react in such a way to curb the impending actual stall. It is, though, obvious that all stall warnings are not true as was the case with the Lion Air 737 MAX involved in the accident, but once a pilot identified a stick shaker to be a nuisance, the next thing he would do is the AIRSPEED UNRELIABLE memory item not runaway stabilizer checklist. Because the AIRSPEED UNRELIABLE checklist puts a nuisance stick shaker to be an indication of unreliable airspeed, a pilot can't be expected to put the trim cut out switches to cut out before dealing with the above procedures unless there is a clear guidance or a QRH procedure addressing such scenario. Third; the third question has to do with the very checklist recommended by the bulletin issued regarding the MCAS system and that is the RUNAWAY STABILIZER checklist.

original_label: EAIB assessment that Boeing's non-response had cascading safety impact

label: High-volume prescribers highly responsive to marketing calls
original_label: High-volume prescribers highly responsive to marketing calls
quote: In September 2010, at a presentation to Purdue's sales supervisors, a Purdue executive explained: 'As I have stated several times, we know increases in the prescriber call average will have the single largest impact of anything you can do to increase prescriptions of Purdue products with our core and super core prescribers.'
context: Purdue executive presentation to sales supervisors in September 2010 explaining internal findings that sales calls directly drive prescriptions from high-volume prescribers.

label: Detailing impact measured by ROI analysis
original_label: Detailing impact measured by ROI analysis
quote: Additionally, Purdue prepared return-on-investment analyses comparing the cost of detailing as compared to the OxyContin prescriptions that would not have been written but for Purdue's in-person marketing, as well as 'sensitivity' analyses showing the impact of Purdue's detailing on OxyContin prescribing.
context: Settlement agreement describing Purdue's quantitative methods to measure the direct causal link between marketing calls and additional prescriptions.

label: FDA approved OxyContin with known abuse risks
original_label: FDA approved OxyContin with known abuse risks
quote: OxyContin is approved by HHS's Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for the management of pain severe enough to require daily, around-the-clock, long-term opioid treatment and for which alternative treatment options are inadequate. It is classified as a Schedule II narcotic under the Controlled Substances Act, 21 U.S.C. § 801 et seq.
context: Settlement agreement recitals establishing FDA's regulatory authority and approval of OxyContin as a Schedule II controlled substance.

label: FDA cautioned reformulated OxyContin not completely tamper-resistant
original_label: FDA cautioned reformulated OxyContin not completely tamper-resistant
quote: Reformulated OxyContin was more difficult to crush or dissolve, but FDA cautioned that Reformulated OxyContin 'is not completely tamper-resistant and those intent on abusing this new formulation will likely find a means to do so. In addition, the product can still be misused or abused and result in overdose by simply administering or ingesting larger than recommended oral doses.'
context: Settlement agreement describing FDA's written warnings about the limits of Reformulated OxyContin's abuse deterrence when approving the product in April 2010.

label: Prior 2007 settlement with Purdue Frederick included CIA
original_label: Prior 2007 settlement with Purdue Frederick included CIA
quote: In 2007, The Purdue Frederick Company, Inc. ('Purdue Frederick'), an affiliate of Purdue, pled guilty to misbranding OxyContin by falsely marketing it as less addictive, less subject to abuse and diversion, and less likely to cause dependence and withdrawal than other pain medications. Purdue and Purdue Frederick also agreed to pay more than $600 million, of which over $100 million was paid to settle civil False Claims Act liability for knowingly causing the submission of false claims to Federal healthcare programs for OxyContin. In conjunction with the resolution, Purdue entered into a five-year Corporate Integrity Agreement with the Department of Health and Human Services, Office of Inspector General (OIG-HHS). OIG-HHS closed the corporate integrity agreement in January 2013.
context: Settlement agreement recitals documenting prior enforcement against Purdue's predecessor for OxyContin misbranding and false claims, including a five-year Corporate Integrity Agreement that ended in 2013.

label: Corporate Integrity Agreement closed without preventing recurrence
original_label: Corporate Integrity Agreement closed without preventing recurrence
quote: In 2007, The Purdue Frederick Company, Inc. ('Purdue Frederick'), an affiliate of Purdue, pled guilty to misbranding OxyContin by falsely marketing it as less addictive, less subject to abuse and diversion, and less likely to cause dependence and withdrawal than other pain medications. Purdue and Purdue Frederick also agreed to pay more than $600 million, of which over $100 million was paid to settle civil False Claims Act liability for knowingly causing the submission of false claims to Federal healthcare programs for OxyContin. In conjunction with the resolution, Purdue entered into a five-year Corporate Integrity Agreement with the Department of Health and Human Services, Office of Inspector General (OIG-HHS). OIG-HHS closed the corporate integrity agreement in January 2013.
context: Settlement agreement noting that OIG-HHS closed its oversight agreement in January 2013, after which Purdue renewed the same conduct from 2013-2018 per the charges.

label: Purdue's ADD program excluded high-volume doctors inconsistently
original_label: Purdue's ADD program excluded high-volume doctors inconsistently
quote: However, high-volume prescribers were often not reported and, even if they were, they were sometimes not added to Region Zero until they lost the ability to prescribe through legal or medical board action. In addition, certain Purdue policies resulted in high-volume prescribers not being reported to ADD, and thus not being added to Region Zero. For example, Purdue trained its sales representatives to only report clear instances of abuse and diversion, and sales representatives were instructed to discuss the reports with their district managers prior to filing. In addition, although Purdue's policy stated that it required timely reporting, Purdue had few, if any, effective compliance measures to address an employee's failure to report, and very few sales representatives were penalized for failing to timely report.
context: Settlement agreement describing how Purdue's internal Abuse and Diversion Detection program was weakened by discretionary reporting, weak enforcement, and delayed placements on its do-not-call list.

label: Purdue sales force incentivized by volume not compliance
original_label: Purdue sales force incentivized by volume not compliance
quote: In turn, sales representatives were rewarded with incentive compensation tied to the volume of OxyContin prescriptions generated from the health care providers they had detailed and faced corrective action plans, such as performance improvement plans, when they did not meet their sales goals.
context: Settlement agreement describing how Purdue's compensation structure directly tied sales representative rewards to prescription volume rather than compliance.

label: OMS Committee continued marketing to suspicious pharmacies
original_label: OMS Committee continued marketing to suspicious pharmacies
quote: Despite having this data, Purdue continued knowingly marketing to the pharmacies that filled the prescriptions of Region Zero and other red flag providers, which led those prescribers' medically unnecessary Purdue prescriptions to be filled.
context: Settlement agreement describing how Purdue's Order Monitoring System Committee, despite having data on pharmacies filling prescriptions from flagged prescribers, allowed marketing to continue.

label: OMS Committee voted to monitor suspicious pharmacy rather than halt
original_label: OMS Committee voted to monitor suspicious pharmacy rather than halt
quote: For example, in or around 2010, Purdue's OMS Committee reviewed a Florida pharmacy based on a report from a district manager that the pharmacy was 'filling primarily from 1.7.1 physicians,' referring to prescribers reported to ADD for displaying indicia of abuse and diversion. The report stated that the Florida pharmacy's 'parking lot is filled with cars with license plates from other states including Kentucky. They are ordering and filling prescriptions for primarily OxyContin 80mg. . . . [They are also filling prescriptions] from 1.7.1 physicians. He asked the pharmacist if he had any concerns about filling prescriptions from these physicians, and the Pharmacist (owner) stated that he was not going to question what a physician writes for his/her patient.' Despite Purdue's knowledge of the red flags indicating the pharmacy was engaged in abuse and diversion, the OMS Committee voted to 'continue to monitor' the pharmacy, and allowed the sales representatives to continue to call on the pharmacy for the next five years through 2015.
context: Settlement agreement describing a specific instance where Purdue's OMS Committee had concrete evidence of suspicious pharmacy activity and continued allowing marketing despite red flags.

category: Legitimate access and separation from victims
label: Sales representatives called on prescribers in person
original_label: Sales representatives called on prescribers in person
quote: Until it stopped marketing opioids in February 2018, Purdue sought to increase and maintain opioid sales by sending sales representatives to prescribers' offices and pharmacies to meet with prescribers in person; deliver company-developed messaging; give the prescribers meals (such as coffee, breakfast, and lunch) and marketing materials (such as articles, brochures, posters, and other media); and provide information about pharmacies stocking Purdue opioids and prescription coverage, including coverage under Federal healthcare benefit programs. This practice is known in the pharmaceutical industry as 'calling on' or 'detailing' healthcare providers and pharmacies.
context: Settlement agreement describing Purdue's routine legitimate sales practice of in-person detailing to prescribers and pharmacies.

category: Legitimate access and separation from victims
label: Purdue collected prescriber data for targeting
original_label: Purdue collected prescriber data for targeting
quote: Purdue executives closely analyzed Purdue's internal data, including data purchased from vendors, in order to target high-volume prescribers and monitor their prescriptions.
context: Settlement agreement describing how Purdue used legitimate commercial data sources to identify and track high-volume prescribers for targeting.

category: Legitimate access and separation from victims
label: Federal healthcare beneficiaries separated from marketing
original_label: Federal healthcare beneficiaries separated from marketing
quote: Purdue knew that it was reasonably foreseeable that its promotional activities for its drugs were a substantial factor in claims being submitted to Federal healthcare programs.
context: Settlement agreement stating that Purdue understood the causal link between its marketing activities and claims submitted to federal programs, despite spatial and temporal separation from beneficiaries.

label: E2E presented as medical best practice optimization
original_label: E2E presented as medical best practice optimization
quote: E2E took a multifaceted approach to increasing OxyContin prescribing and Purdue's profits. The consulting company recommended, among other strategies, refreshing Purdue's marketing messaging – particularly around titration to higher, more lucrative dosages - and undertaking strategies to ensure prescriptions would be filled. At its core, however, E2E focused on intensifying marketing to the very highest-volume prescribers in the country by targeting them with increased frequency and minimizing sales representative discretion in identifying prescribers to target.
context: Settlement agreement describing how E2E was framed as medical optimization while its core function was to intensify marketing to concentrated high-volume prescribers.

label: Sales scripts pivoted from addiction safety concerns to medical language
original_label: Sales scripts pivoted from addiction safety concerns to medical language
quote: In addition, representatives were trained to '[o]vercome . . . objection[s]' raised by providers and get physicians to 'commit' to prescribe more Purdue products. Specifically, representatives were trained to pivot from legitimate physician concerns about addiction to statements about 'dependence' and opioid 'tolerance.' When asked about the safety of high dosages, representatives were instructed to respond that OxyContin 'does not have a ceiling dose.'
context: Settlement agreement describing how Purdue trained sales representatives to reframe safety objections using medical terminology rather than addressing addiction risks.

label: Titration marketing encouraged higher dosages with medical framing
original_label: Titration marketing encouraged higher dosages with medical framing
quote: For example, a 2011 script stated: 'We discussed the discontinuation rate of extended-release opioids by day 35. One of the potential reasons for discontinuation is the lack of efficacy perhaps as a result of lack of titration.' E2E created a refreshed 2014 version of the script that stated: 'According to an analysis … 57% of patients initiated on some commonly prescribed extended-release opioids are no longer on those products by day 35,' 'Assuming a patient discontinues therapy by day 35 due to their perceived lack of pain relief, what is the impact on your patient, you and your staff? (pause for effect),' and then 'Doctor, working with you and your staff, I can provide support to you when initiating and titrating dosages on my products.'
context: Settlement agreement showing how Purdue's sales scripts used clinical statistics and medical framing to encourage prescribers to increase dosages.

label: Pain CDS alert presented as neutral clinical decision support
original_label: Pain CDS alert presented as neutral clinical decision support
quote: The Pain CDS was presented to providers as a neutral medical standard. However, Purdue's primary objective in designing of the CDS alert was to increase its ERO sales, and the Pain CDS deviated from medically accepted standards, CDC guidelines, and FDA-approved labels for Purdue's EROs.
context: Settlement agreement describing how Purdue's electronic health record intervention was designed to appear as neutral clinical guidance while optimized for drug sales.

label: Practice Fusion CDS included unapproved treatment recommendations
original_label: Practice Fusion CDS included unapproved treatment recommendations
quote: In creating a list of treatment plan options for addressing pain, Purdue employees pulled from a list of alternatives treatments to opioids in a New England Medical Journal article on opioid abuse in chronic pain. That article described several concerns about opioid use, including 'concerns about overdosing and abuse by patients' and '[f]actors associated with the risk of opioid overdose or addiction.' Despite this, Purdue employees added opioids to the list within the CDS of potential therapies for chronic pain.
context: Settlement agreement showing how Purdue selectively incorporated medical literature while adding opioids to the treatment options list despite acknowledged risks.

label: Speaker programs selected doctors with high prescribing based on sales data
original_label: Speaker programs selected doctors with high prescribing based on sales data
quote: Purdue allowed its sales and marketing personnel, who had data on each doctor's prescribing of Purdue's drugs and whose compensation depended on increasing their assigned doctors' prescribing of Purdue's drugs, to select speakers instead of Purdue's medical education staff. Purdue also allowed its sales representatives to relay and endorse doctors' requests to be retained, and the doctors could be selected even if they had not been identified by the consulting company Purdue had retained for this purpose. Within Purdue, these were known as 'unsolicited requests.' Purdue vested final authority to select doctors in Purdue's Marketing department, which had data on each doctor's Purdue prescriptions.
context: Settlement agreement describing how Purdue's speaker program selection process was controlled by sales and marketing personnel with financial incentives and prescribing data.

label: Specialty pharmacy payments tied to volume and styled as fair market
original_label: Specialty pharmacy payments tied to volume and styled as fair market
quote: The agreements Purdue ultimately entered into with three specialty pharmacies made payments at above fair market value that were tied to the volume of Hysingla the pharmacy dispensed.
context: Settlement agreement describing how Purdue structured pharmacy payments to increase with drug volume while framed as commercial agreements.

label: Purdue anticipated pharmacy safeguard timing and response
original_label: Purdue anticipated pharmacy safeguard timing and response
quote: As noted above, in July 2013, as part of the E2E program, the consulting company relayed to Purdue and the Board that OxyContin revenues were down because, among other things, 'entire pharmacies [are] being shut off by distributors, pharmacies themselves imposing tablet limits, decreases in channel inventory leading to greater stockouts, and pharmacies choosing to not stock OxyContin.'
context: Settlement agreement describing how Purdue understood specific pharmacy and distributor safeguards that were reducing OxyContin sales and designed E2E partly to circumvent them.

label: Purdue identified predictable pharmacy good faith dispensing policies
original_label: Purdue identified predictable pharmacy good faith dispensing policies
quote: On November 18, 2013, Purdue received a presentation from a vendor that identified the top twenty OxyContin prescribers whose OxyContin prescriptions declined as a result of a pharmacy's 'good faith dispensing' policy designed to hinder the dispensing of medically unnecessary prescriptions.
context: Settlement agreement showing Purdue received specific data on which prescribers' sales were blocked by predictable pharmacy safeguard policies.

label: Board received budget information on declining sales
original_label: Board received budget information on declining sales
quote: Purdue management presented information regarding the slipping demand for Purdue's OxyContin to Purdue's Board in December 2010, showing that the total weekly kilograms dispensed of branded OxyContin declined from August to November 2010.
context: Settlement agreement documenting that the Board received information about sales decline following reformulation in December 2010.

label: Board received detailed analysis of abuse and diversion decline
original_label: Board received detailed analysis of abuse and diversion decline
quote: The materials provided to the Board in October 2011 also included a study, 'Changes in Prescribing Patterns Following Introduction of Reformulated OxyContin: A Window into Diversion.' The study examined a two-year period, August 2009 to July 2011, and found that data for Region Zero prescribers showed an 86% decline in their OxyContin prescriptions after Purdue's introduction of its reformulated version, and especially at the highest dosages, 40 and 80 mg tablets.
context: Settlement agreement showing the Board received a detailed study analyzing how reformulation reduced abuse by Region Zero prescribers in October 2011.

label: Board approved E2E implementation with full knowledge
original_label: Board approved E2E implementation with full knowledge
quote: On August 23, 2013, certain Sackler family members met with the consulting company and examined its 'unvarnished' findings and recommendations. Following the meeting, one of the consulting company partners that led the meeting with the Sacklers memorialized in an email: '[T]he room was filled with only family, including the elder statesman Dr. Raymond [Sackler]. . . . We went through exhibit by exhibit for about 2 hrs. . . . They were extremely supportive of the findings and our recommendations . . . and wanted to strongly endorse getting going on our recommendations.' Another consulting company partner further remarked in the email correspondence that their 'findings were crystal clear to' the Sacklers 'and [the Sacklers] gave a ringing endorsement of 'moving forward fast.'
context: Settlement agreement documenting that Sackler family board members met directly with consultants, reviewed unvarnished findings about targeting high-volume prescribers, and gave enthusiastic approval to implement E2E.

label: Board received information on E2E call frequency and effectiveness
original_label: Board received information on E2E call frequency and effectiveness
quote: An email between two Purdue executives dated October 23, 2013, entitled 'S&P Final Version' attached Board presentations, a 2014 Budget Presentation to the Board on OxyContin Tablets, which reflected that the extreme high-volume prescribers that E2E targeted were most sensitive to Purdue's marketing: Increased calls with decile 8-10 prescribers have a significant impact on OxyContin®TRx growth. Growth In OxyContin [by] prescriber by# of PDEs received.
context: Settlement agreement showing the Board received a 2014 budget presentation with data demonstrating the high responsiveness of top-decile prescribers to increased sales calls.

label: Board decision on alternative distribution strategy
original_label: Board decision on alternative distribution strategy
quote: On August 16, 2013, one day after the Board briefing on E2E discussed above, Mortimer D. A. Sackler emailed a Purdue executive and others asking what ideas management had for creating a new distribution system 'to help relieve this problem of product access for legitimate chronic pain patients,' which would use 'an independent service to verify the legitimacy of [the patients'] prescriptions.' Two days later, Mortimer D.A. Sackler reiterated, 'I do think there may be an opportunity here for us to set up a complimentary business to handle this for Purdue as well as other controlled drug manufacturers. Do we have a team who could explore this possibility?'
context: Settlement agreement showing Sackler family members, as board members, directly directed management to develop new distribution channels to circumvent pharmacy safeguards.

label: Sales representatives instructed on Region Zero do-not-call policy
original_label: Sales representatives instructed on Region Zero do-not-call policy
quote: Purdue sales representatives were trained to report prescribers suspected of abuse and diversion to ADD, and some sales representatives did so.
context: Settlement agreement noting that Purdue had trained sales representatives to report suspected abuse, indicating some internal control structure existed.

label: Reformulated OxyContin sales declined post-launch
original_label: Reformulated OxyContin sales declined post-launch
quote: Shortly after the introduction of Reformulated OxyContin, Purdue's profits declined, in large part, because some individuals who abused OxyContin moved to more easily manipulated opioids.
context: Settlement agreement describing how Purdue's strategy to implement reformulated OxyContin in August 2010 had an unintended consequence of reducing abuse but also reducing profits.

label: Department of Justice filed fraud claims in bankruptcy
original_label: Department of Justice filed fraud claims in bankruptcy
quote: On July 30, 2020, the United States Department of Justice submitted claim 137848 in the bankruptcy of Purdue on behalf of HHS, DHA, and OPM alleging that, from 2010 to 2018, Purdue knowingly caused false, medically unnecessary claims to be submitted to federal health care programs for Purdue's opioid drugs; from 2008 to 2018, Purdue transferred billions of dollars in distributions and assets to its owners, the Sackler family and their holding companies and trusts, some of which is recoverable as fraudulent transfers; and Purdue's misconduct gives rise to criminal liability and forfeiture of proceeds traceable to Purdue's crimes.
context: Settlement agreement recitals documenting that the DOJ submitted fraud and false claims charges against Purdue in bankruptcy court on July 30, 2020.

label: Purdue agreed to guilty plea to three felony counts
original_label: Purdue agreed to guilty plea to three felony counts
quote: On such date as may be determined by the U.S. District Court for the District of New Jersey, pursuant to Rule 11(c)(1)(C) of the Federal Rules of Criminal Procedure, Purdue will plead guilty to a three-count Information to be filed by the United States in United States v. Purdue Pharma L.P., Criminal Action No. [to be determined] (D.N.J.) that will allege violations of 18 U.S.C. § 371 for: (1) a dual-object conspiracy to defraud the United States and to violate the Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act, 21 U.S.C. § 331, 353; (2) a conspiracy to violate the Anti-Kickback Statute (AKS), 42 U.S.C. § 1320a-7b(b), related to Purdue's payments to health care providers; and (3) a conspiracy to violate the AKS related to Purdue's payments to Practice Fusion, a cloud-based electronic health records platform (hereinafter the 'Criminal Action').
context: Settlement agreement describing Purdue's agreement to plead guilty to three felony counts including fraud, false claims, and kickback conspiracy.

label: Purdue excluded from federal healthcare programs
original_label: Purdue excluded from federal healthcare programs
quote: Purdue understands and acknowledges that as a result of the guilty plea described in Paragraph H of the Preamble above, it will be excluded pursuant to 42 U.S.C. 1320a-7(a)(1) from Medicare, Medicaid, and all other Federal health care programs, as defined in 42 U.S.C. § 1320a-7b(f). Such exclusion shall have national effect and, pursuant to 42 U.S.C. § 1320a-7(i), shall be effective after a judgment of conviction has been entered or a guilty plea has been accepted by a Federal, state, or local court.
context: Settlement agreement establishing that Purdue's guilty plea triggers mandatory exclusion from all federal healthcare programs.

label: CFO establishes and operates private equity funds transacting with Enron
original_label: CFO establishes and operates private equity funds transacting with Enron
quote: Despite clear conflicts of interest, the Enron Board of Directors approved an unprecedented arrangement allowing Enron's Chief Financial Officer to establish and operate the LJM private equity funds which transacted business with Enron and profited at Enron's expense.
context: The Subcommittee finding states the core wrongdoing: Fastow used his CFO position to create and control LJM partnerships that profited from Enron.

label: Enron management orchestrated high-risk accounting and off-the-books activity
original_label: Enron management orchestrated high-risk accounting and off-the-books activity
quote: While the evidence indicates that, in some instances, Enron Board members were misinformed or misled, the Subcommittee investigation found that overall the Board received substantial information about Enron's plans and activities and explicitly authorized or allowed many of the questionable Enron strategies, policies, and transactions now subject to criticism. Enron's high-risk accounting practices, for example, were not hidden from the Board. The Board knew of them and took no action to prevent Enron from using them.
context: The Subcommittee assessment shows that Enron management actively pursued high-risk accounting as strategy, not concealment.

label: Senior officers profited from LJM partnerships at Enron's expense
original_label: Senior officers profited from LJM partnerships at Enron's expense
quote: Mr. Fastow told the Board that he had earned $45 million on a $5 million investment in LJM1 and LJM2 in just 2 years. Other Enron employees also admitted to significant LJM returns in a short period, including two who received immediate returns of $1 million each on individual investments of $5,800.
context: The Subcommittee documents the financial incentives that motivated Fastow and other senior Enron officers to use their positions to extract value through LJM.

label: Kenneth Lay used CEO credit line to extract cash and stock sales
original_label: Kenneth Lay used CEO credit line to extract cash and stock sales
quote: In the 1-year period from October 2000 to October 2001, Mr. Lay used the credit line to obtain over $77 million in cash from the company and repaid the loans exclusively with Enron stock. Several directors confirmed that Mr. Lay still owed the company about $7 million.
context: The Subcommittee documents Lay's systematic abuse of his CEO position and the credit line it gave him access to.

label: Shareholders dependent on financial statements for investment decisions
original_label: Shareholders dependent on financial statements for investment decisions
quote: Thousands of Enron employees lost not only their jobs but a significant part of their retirement savings; Enron shareholders saw the value of their investments plummet; and hundreds, if not thousands of businesses around the world, were turned into Enron creditors in bankruptcy court likely to receive only pennies on the dollars owed to them.
context: The Subcommittee describes who was harmed, establishing shareholders and employees as targets who relied on Enron's representations.

label: Investors cannot detect harm from off-balance-sheet accounting
original_label: Investors cannot detect harm from off-balance-sheet accounting
quote: The Enron Board failed to provide that motivation. Once public disclosure was made of Enron's off-the-books activities and liabilities, credit rating agencies, financial analysts, and investors began to reconsider their view of the company, and many investors reacted by selling Enron stock. Enron's hidden activities and liabilities clearly damaged investor confidence in the company and contributed to its collapse.
context: The Subcommittee shows that investors could not detect the off-the-books activity until it was publicly disclosed, making them a suitable target.

label: Creditors and business partners relied on Enron's financial condition representation
original_label: Creditors and business partners relied on Enron's financial condition representation
quote: Hundreds, if not thousands of businesses around the world, were turned into Enron creditors in bankruptcy court likely to receive only pennies on the dollars owed to them.
context: The Subcommittee identifies creditors and business partners as vulnerable targets dependent on Enron's financial reporting.

label: SEC could have detected disclosure inadequacy but lacked enforcement
original_label: SEC could have detected disclosure inadequacy but lacked enforcement
quote: The Enron Board failed to provide that motivation. Once public disclosure was made of Enron's off-the-books activities and liabilities, credit rating agencies, financial analysts, and investors began to reconsider their view of the company.
context: The Subcommittee implies the SEC should have reviewed Enron's disclosures in 10-K and proxy filings as a capable guardian.

label: Andersen auditors had knowledge and mandate to prevent accounting fraud
original_label: Andersen auditors had knowledge and mandate to prevent accounting fraud
quote: Andersen's 1999 and 2000 client risk analyses placed Enron in its category for 'Maximum' risk. The 2000 analysis, which was signed by David Duncan and four other Andersen partners, identified several 'Risk Drivers' for Enron, including stating that Enron 'Management Pressures' were 'Very Significant' and that the 'Accounting and Financial Reporting Risk' associated with Enron was also 'Very Significant.'
context: The Subcommittee documents that Andersen possessed expertise and information to detect high-risk accounting at Enron.

label: Credit rating agencies had access to financial information and downgrade power
original_label: Credit rating agencies had access to financial information and downgrade power
quote: In order to ensure an investment-grade credit rating, Enron began to emphasize increasing its cash flow, lowering its debt, and smoothing its earnings on its financial statements to meet the criteria set by credit rating agencies like Moody's and Standard & Poor's.
context: The Subcommittee shows that credit rating agencies were powerful guardians with information access and the ability to downgrade.

label: Board delegates control oversight to management and Andersen
original_label: Board delegates control oversight to management and Andersen
quote: The Board relied on Enron management to develop and implement the day-to-day controls needed to monitor LJM, and limited its own oversight to less frequent and more generalized reviews.
context: The Subcommittee documents how the Board abdicated its guardian role by delegating oversight to those being overseen.

label: Board waives ethics code for CFO to create private equity fund
original_label: Board waives ethics code for CFO to create private equity fund
quote: Enron's code of conduct for its employees expressly prohibited Enron employees from obtaining personal financial gain from a company doing business with Enron. This prohibition could be waived, however, by the CEO upon a finding that a proposed arrangement would 'not adversely affect the best interests of the Company.' In the case of the LJM partnerships, Mr. Lay approved waiving the code of conduct prohibition for Mr. Fastow, but also asked the Enron Board to ratify his decision, even though Board concurrence was not explicitly required by company rules.
context: The Subcommittee documents how the Board explicitly waived its own governance safeguard to enable Fastow's conflicted arrangement.

label: Audit Committee accepts Andersen independence despite massive consulting fees
original_label: Audit Committee accepts Andersen independence despite massive consulting fees
quote: Enron Board members told the Subcommittee staff that they had been unaware of any tensions between Andersen and Enron and unaware of the many concerns Andersen had with Enron's accounting practices. A number of the interviewed directors discounted the importance of Andersen's fees, even though Enron was one of Andersen's largest clients and, during 2000, paid Andersen about $52 million or $1 million per week for its work. Andersen's consulting fees at Enron exceeded its auditing fees for the first time in 1999, and, in 2000, totaled about $27 million compared to auditing fees of about $25 million.
context: The Subcommittee shows the Audit Committee failed to recognize that massive consulting fees compromised Andersen's independence as guardian.

label: Andersen internally documented concerns but gave clean audit opinion
original_label: Andersen internally documented concerns but gave clean audit opinion
quote: An email dated February 6, 2001, sent to David Duncan and Thomas Bauer by another Andersen partner, Michael D. Jones, offers further proof that Andersen viewed Enron as engaged in risky accounting. This email summarizes a meeting held the previous day by 14 senior Andersen partners to decide whether the firm should retain Enron as a client. The email indicates that the group was aware of and uneasy about a number of accounting practices and transactions at Enron. Ultimately, the conclusion was reached to retain Enron as a client citing that it appeared that we had the appropriate people and processes in place to serve Enron and manage our engagement risks.
context: The Subcommittee documents that Andersen knew of high-risk practices but chose not to warn the Board or withdraw as auditor.

label: Board directors have financial ties to Enron reducing independence
original_label: Board directors have financial ties to Enron reducing independence
quote: Since 1996, Enron paid a monthly retainer of $6,000 to Lord John Wakeham for consulting services, in addition to his Board compensation. In 2000, Enron paid him $72,000 for his consulting work alone. Since 1991, Enron paid Board member John A. Urquhart for consulting services, in addition to his Board compensation. In 2000, Enron paid Mr. Urquhart $493,914 for his consulting work alone.
context: The Subcommittee identifies financial ties that weakened multiple Board members' ability to provide independent oversight.

label: Audit Committee chair rarely contacted auditor outside of meetings
original_label: Audit Committee chair rarely contacted auditor outside of meetings
quote: The Audit Committee had very limited contact with Andersen, essentially communicating with Andersen personnel only at Board meetings. The Audit Committee Chairman for more than 10 years was Dr. Jaedicke. Despite his long tenure on the Audit Committee, the interviews disclosed that Dr. Jaedicke had 'rarely' had any contact with Andersen outside of an official Audit Committee or Board meeting. None of the other interviewed Audit Committee members had ever contacted anyone from Andersen regarding Enron outside of an official Enron Committee or Board meeting. None had ever telephoned Andersen directly.
context: The Subcommittee shows the Audit Committee failed to develop independent communication channels with the auditor.

label: Board integrated Andersen auditing with consulting, removing independence
original_label: Board integrated Andersen auditing with consulting, removing independence
quote: The Audit Committee members indicated that they had thought Andersen and Enron had a good working relationship, and taken great comfort in knowing that Andersen was more than Enron's outside auditor, but also provided Enron with extensive internal auditing and consulting services, combining its roles into what Enron called 'an integrated audit.' Dr. Jaedicke maintained that it was a significant benefit to Enron for Andersen to be involved with Enron's activities on a day-to-day basis and to help the company design its most complex transactions from the start.
context: The Subcommittee documents how the Board explicitly welcomed Andersen's dual role, eliminating arm's-length auditor independence.

label: Board approves major transactions exceeding dollar thresholds
original_label: Board approves major transactions exceeding dollar thresholds
quote: The Finance Committee was responsible for approving major transactions which, in 2001, met or exceeded $75 million in value. It also reviewed transactions valued between $25 million and $75 million; oversaw Enron's risk management efforts; and provided guidance on the company's financial decisions and policies.
context: The Subcommittee describes the Board's formal transaction approval process, showing predictable thresholds that could be gamed.

label: Board meetings limited to 1-2 hours despite complex transactions
original_label: Board meetings limited to 1-2 hours despite complex transactions
quote: The Board normally met five times during the year, with additional special meetings as needed. Board meetings usually lasted 2 days, with the first day devoted to Committee meetings and a Board dinner, and the second day devoted to a meeting of the full Board. Committee meetings generally lasted between 1 and 2 hours and were arranged to allow Board members, who typically sat on three Committees, to attend all assigned Committee meetings. Full Board meetings also generally lasted between 1 and 2 hours.
context: The Subcommittee documents the predictable, time-constrained Board meeting routine that limited ability to scrutinize transactions.

label: LJM1 approved quickly before quarter-end reporting deadline
original_label: LJM1 approved quickly before quarter-end reporting deadline
quote: Enron obtained Board approval of LJM1's formation and the Rhythms transaction on June 28, 2 days prior to the end of the reporting period on June 30.
context: The Subcommittee shows that Enron management exploited the Board's predictable need to close transactions before quarter-end.

label: LJM2 presentation to Finance Committee lasted 90 minutes
original_label: LJM2 presentation to Finance Committee lasted 90 minutes
quote: Due to Mr. Fastow's participation, the Board was asked to ratify a second code of conduct waiver that would allow him to set up and manage LJM2, hold an ownership interest in the fund, locate additional investors and financing, and receive compensation for his efforts. This time the LJM2 proposal went first to the Finance Committee, which approved it in a 90-minute meeting on October 11, 1999, after what Mr. Winokur, the Committee Chairman, described as 'a vigorous discussion.'
context: The Subcommittee shows the Finance Committee's predictable time constraint, followed by Mr. Fastow acting as if approval was certain.

label: Audit Committee annual LJM review spent 15-30 minutes on single sheet
original_label: Audit Committee annual LJM review spent 15-30 minutes on single sheet
quote: At the first review in 2000, the Audit Committee was given a single sheet of paper listing the names of eight transactions that LJM had entered into with Enron in 1999. The only information provided for each transaction was the name of the 'investment,' the transaction's approximate dollar value, and a description of the transaction in ten words or less. The Committee spent between 15 and 30 minutes reviewing the list with Mr. Causey. The Audit Committee did not go into the details of any specific transaction, nor did it review any Deal Approval Sheet (DASH) or LJM Approval Sheet, even though these documents were typically only a few pages long and would have provided key information.
context: The Subcommittee documents the Audit Committee's predictable superficial review routine that could easily be satisfied with minimal information.

label: Board Audit Committee chartered to review accounting and auditor independence
original_label: Board Audit Committee chartered to review accounting and auditor independence
quote: The charter of the Enron Audit Committee explicitly requires the Committee to ensure the independence of the company's auditors, assess Enron's internal controls and the quality of its financial reporting, and review Enron's financial statements. According to the charter, the Audit Committee's 'principal functions' also include: '[d]iscuss[ing] with the independent auditor information relating to the auditor's judgements about the quality of the Company's accounting principles, including . . . the clarity and completeness of the Company's accounting information contained in the financial statements'; determin[ing] whether Enron's 'internal financial controls . . . provide reasonable assurance that the Company's publicly reported financial statements are presented fairly in conformity with generally accepted accounting principles'; and '[a]pprov[ing] major changes and other major questions of choice regarding the appropriate accounting principles and practices to be followed when preparing the Company's financial statement for the purpose of making recommendations to the Board of Directors as necessary.'
context: The Subcommittee shows the Audit Committee had formal charter responsibilities for the exact areas where control failed.

label: Board Finance Committee authorized to approve transactions and oversee LJM
original_label: Board Finance Committee authorized to approve transactions and oversee LJM
quote: The Finance Committee was responsible for approving major transactions which, in 2001, met or exceeded $75 million in value. It also reviewed transactions valued between $25 million and $75 million; oversaw Enron's risk management efforts; and provided guidance on the company's financial decisions and policies.
context: The Subcommittee identifies the Finance Committee's formal mandate to oversee the transactions and entities that enabled wrongdoing.

label: Compensation Committee approved executive compensation plans with little debate
original_label: Compensation Committee approved executive compensation plans with little debate
quote: The Enron Board, through its Compensation Committee, was not only informed of the company's lavish executive compensation plans, it apparently approved them with little debate or restraint.
context: The Subcommittee documents that the Compensation Committee failed to exercise its control function over compensation incentives.

label: Enron management to implement day-to-day LJM transaction controls
original_label: Enron management to implement day-to-day LJM transaction controls
quote: The Board relied on Enron management to develop and implement the day-to-day controls needed to monitor LJM, and limited its own oversight to less frequent and more generalized reviews. The nature and extent of the LJM controls actually put into place by Enron management varied over time. The original LJM1 presentation in June 1999 did not specify any controls. The LJM2 presentation in October 1999 specified just one control—that Chief Accounting Officer Richard Causey 'approve all transactions between Enron and LJM.'
context: The Subcommittee shows the Board delegated its oversight of LJM controls to the management actors with conflicts of interest.

label: LJM transaction approval process poorly designed and inconsistently followed
original_label: LJM transaction approval process poorly designed and inconsistently followed
quote: The Powers Report found, however, that 'the process was not well-designed, and it was not consistently followed.' Some LJM transactions took place without any DASH or LJM Approval Sheet, others relied on a DASH or LJM Approval Sheet that did not contain the required signatures, and still other deals were closed before the documentation was completed. The Powers Report found that, in at least 13 instances, the persons negotiating the Enron-LJM deals—on both sides of the table—reported to Mr. Fastow, and that Mr. Fastow, on occasion, 'pressur[ed]' them 'to obtain better terms for LJM.'
context: The Subcommittee documents that the internal controls were structurally flawed and breached by those responsible for implementing them.

label: Compensation Committee failed to obtain information on Fastow LJM compensation
original_label: Compensation Committee failed to obtain information on Fastow LJM compensation
quote: Dr. LeMaistre, then Chairman of the Compensation Committee, was present at the Finance Committee meeting, and attempted to obtain the requested information on Mr. Fastow's LJM compensation. He indicated during his interview and at the hearing that, after the Finance Committee meeting, he asked Enron's senior compensation officer, Mary Joyce, to provide him with information on the outside income of all of Enron's '16(b) officers,' a reference to top company officials identified according to an SEC regulation. He said during his Subcommittee interview that he did not specifically name Mr. Fastow to Ms. Joyce because he did not want to start any office gossip. Ms. Joyce did not provide him with the information he requested. He said that he asked her a second time to obtain the information, but she again did not do so. He admitted that he never actually named Mr. Fastow to her or insisted that she obtain information about his LJM compensation. Instead, Dr. LeMaistre let the matter drop.
context: The Subcommittee documents how the internal control handler gave up when not immediately satisfied, allowing the wrongdoing to continue undetected.

original_label: CFO legitimate access to valuation methodologies and asset information
quote: The arrangement essentially permitted Enron's top financial control officer—an individual with personal knowledge of Enron's assets, liabilities and profit margins—to set up his own company and sit on both sides of the table in negotiations between his business and his employer.
context: The Subcommittee describes how Fastow's legitimate CFO position gave him superior information and access to both sides of LJM transactions.

category: Legitimate access and separation from victims

original_label: Board routine access to financial statements and transaction approvals

original_label: Enron management designed complex transactions and presented to Board
