label: Crash test revealed vulnerability; design exposed thousands to hazard
original_label: Crash test revealed vulnerability; design exposed thousands to hazard
quote: Through the results of the crash tests Ford knew that the Pinto's fuel tank and rear structure would expose consumers to serious injury or death in a 20- to 30-mile-per-hour collision. Unlike malicious conduct directed toward a single specific individual, Ford's tortious conduct endangered the lives of thousands of Pinto purchasers.
context: Court's assessment of the scope and nature of harm created by the defective design affecting mass market consumers.

label: Federal regulation required fuel system integrity standard
original_label: Federal regulation required fuel system integrity standard
quote: Ford also conducted the tests to see if the Pinto as designed would meet a proposed federal regulation requiring all automobiles manufactured in 1972 to be able to withstand a 20-mile-per-hour fixed barrier impact without significant fuel spillage and all automobiles manufactured after January 1, 1973, to withstand a 30-mile-per-hour fixed barrier impact without significant fuel spillage.
context: Court describing the federal regulatory framework that established safety standards Ford was expected to meet.

label: No fuel integrity standard at time of Pinto design
original_label: No fuel integrity standard at time of Pinto design
quote: It was then the preferred practice in Europe and Japan to locate the gas tank over the rear axle in subcompacts because a small vehicle has less 'crush space' between the rear axle and the bumper than larger cars. The Pinto's styling, however, required the tank to be placed behind the rear axle leaving only 9 or 10 inches of 'crush space'--far less than in any other American automobile or Ford overseas subcompact.
context: Court explaining the design choice that created vulnerability, noting the absence of regulatory requirements at the time that might have forced compliance with safer practices known internationally.

label: Proposed standard allowed time to avoid compliance investment
original_label: Proposed standard allowed time to avoid compliance investment
quote: Ford also conducted the tests to see if the Pinto as designed would meet a proposed federal regulation requiring all automobiles manufactured in 1972 to be able to withstand a 20-mile-per-hour fixed barrier impact without significant fuel spillage and all automobiles manufactured after January 1, 1973, to withstand a 30-mile-per-hour fixed barrier impact without significant fuel spillage. The crash tests revealed that the Pinto's fuel system as designed could not meet the 20-mile-per-hour proposed standard.
context: Court describing how the proposed regulation's delayed effective date (January 1, 1973 for stricter standard) created a window during which Pinto could be sold without required modifications.

label: Regulatory delay in fuel standard adoption created compliance window
original_label: Regulatory delay in fuel standard adoption created compliance window
quote: At an April 1971 product review meeting chaired by Mr. MacDonald, those present received and discussed a report (exhibit 125) prepared by Ford engineers pertaining to the financial impact of a proposed federal standard on fuel system integrity and the cost savings which would accrue from deferring even minimal 'fixes.' The report refers to crash tests of the integrity of the fuel system of Ford vehicles and design changes needed to meet anticipated federal standards. Also in evidence was a September 23, 1970, report (exhibit 124) by Ford's 'Chassis Design Office' concerning a program 'to establish a corporate [Ford] position and reply to the government' on the proposed federal fuel system integrity stand ard which included zero fuel spillage at 20 miles per hour fixed barrier crash by January 1, 1972, and 30 miles per hour by January 1, 1973.
context: Court documents showing Ford's internal planning explicitly calculated cost savings from delaying safety fixes until the regulatory deadlines, indicating exploitation of the known timeline of regulatory phaseins.

label: Product review meetings as internal approval checkpoints
original_label: Product review meetings as internal approval checkpoints
quote: During the course of the project, regular product review meetings were held which were chaired by Mr. MacDonald and attended by Mr. Alexander. As the project approached actual production, the engineers responsible for the components of the project 'signed off' to their immediate supervisors who in turn 'signed off' to their superiors and so on up the chain of command until the entire project was approved for public release by Vice Presidents Alexander and MacDonald and ultimately by Mr. Iacocca. The Pinto crash tests results had been forwarded up the chain of command to the ultimate decision-makers and were known to the Ford officials who decided to go forward with production.
context: Court describing Ford's internal approval hierarchy and the chain of command through which safety information was supposed to be reviewed before production decisions.

label: Crash test results reported to engineers and supervisors
original_label: Crash test results reported to engineers and supervisors
quote: Mr. Kennedy, who succeeded Mr. Copp as the engineer in charge of Ford's crash testing program, admitted that the test results had been forwarded up the chain of command to his superiors.
context: Testimony from Ford's own crash testing program director confirming that safety test results were communicated up the management hierarchy.

label: Engineering concerns raised to management but overridden
original_label: Engineering concerns raised to management but overridden
quote: In these conversations, both men expressed concern about the integrity of the Pinto's fuel system and complained about management's unwillingness to deviate from the design if the change would cost money.
context: Evidence that internal safety advocates (engineers) voiced concerns but management prioritized cost savings over safety.

category: Legitimate access and separation from victims
label: Routine business channel: engineering review and production approval
original_label: Routine business channel: engineering review and production approval
quote: During the course of the project, regular product review meetings were held which were chaired by Mr. MacDonald and attended by Mr. Alexander. As the project approached actual production, the engineers responsible for the components of the project 'signed off' to their immediate supervisors who in turn 'signed off' to their superiors and so on up the chain of command until the entire project was approved for public release by Vice Presidents Alexander and MacDonald and ultimately by Mr. Iacocca.
context: Court describing the normal organizational processes through which decisions to proceed with production were made, showing wrongdoing occurred within routine governance channels.

category: Legitimate access and separation from victims
label: Crash testing conducted as ordinary engineering practice
original_label: Crash testing conducted as ordinary engineering practice
quote: During the development of the Pinto, prototypes were built and tested. Some were 'mechanical prototypes' which duplicated mechanical features of the design but not its appearance while others, referred to as 'engineering prototypes,' were true duplicates of the design car. These prototypes as well as two production Pintos were crash tested by Ford to determine, among other things, the integrity of the fuel system in rear-end accidents.
context: Court describing crash testing as a standard engineering development practice that provided legitimate access to knowledge of the defect.

label: Cost-benefit analysis framed as legitimate engineering decision
original_label: Cost-benefit analysis framed as legitimate engineering decision
quote: At an April 1971 product review meeting chaired by Mr. MacDonald, those present received and discussed a report (exhibit 125) prepared by Ford engineers pertaining to the financial impact of a proposed federal standard on fuel system integrity and the cost savings which would accrue from deferring even minimal 'fixes.'
context: Court documenting how Ford's internal reports framed the decision to defer safety fixes as a legitimate financial and regulatory planning exercise.

label: Standard engineering alternatives existed but characterized as deferrable
original_label: Standard engineering alternatives existed but characterized as deferrable
quote: The report states in part: 'The 20 and 30 mph rear fixed barrier crashes will probably require repackaging the fuel tanks in a protected area such as above the rear axle. This is based on moving barrier crash tests of a Chevelle and a Ford at 30 mph and other Ford products at 20 mph. Currently there are no plans for forward models to repackage the fuel tanks. Tests must be conducted to prove that repackaged tanks will live without significantly strengthening rear structure for added protection.' The report also notes that the Pinto was the '[smallest] car line with most difficulty in achieving compliance.'
context: Court documents showing Ford's internal communications acknowledged feasible design solutions while framing them as optional pending further testing.

label: Management decision based on cost savings characterized as business judgment
original_label: Management decision based on cost savings characterized as business judgment
quote: Harley Copp, a former Ford engineer and executive in charge of the crash testing program, testified that the highest level of Ford's management made the decision to go forward with the production of the Pinto, knowing that the gas tank was vulnerable to puncture and rupture at low rear impact speeds creating a significant risk of death or injury from fire and knowing that 'fixes' were feasible at nominal cost. He testified that management's decision was based on the cost savings which would inure from omitting or delaying the 'fixes.'
context: Testimony describing how Ford executives framed their decision to proceed with a known defect as a cost-based business judgment.

label: Crash test evidence created permanent record of known defect
original_label: Crash test evidence created permanent record of known defect
quote: The crash tests revealed that the Pinto's fuel system as designed could not meet the 20-mile-per-hour proposed standard. Mechanical prototypes struck from the rear with a moving barrier at 21 miles per hour caused the fuel tank to be driven forward and to be punctured, causing fuel leakage in excess of the standard prescribed by the proposed regulation. A production Pinto crash tested at 21 miles per hour into a fixed barrier caused the fuel neck to be torn from the gas tank and the tank to be punctured by a bolt head on the differential housing. In at least one test, spilled fuel entered the driver's compartment through gaps resulting from the separation of the seams joining the rear wheel wells to the floor pan.
context: Court describing multiple crash tests that documented the defect in the fuel system, creating objective evidence later used to prove Ford's knowledge.

label: Accident provided evidence of design defect causing severe burns
original_label: Accident provided evidence of design defect causing severe burns
quote: A 1972 Ford Pinto hatchback automobile unexpectedly stalled on a freeway, erupting into flames when it was rear ended by a car proceeding in the same direction. Mrs. Lilly Gray, the driver of the Pinto, suffered fatal burns and 13-year-old Richard Grimshaw, a passenger in the Pinto, suffered severe and permanently disfiguring burns on his face and entire body. Grimshaw and the heirs of Mrs. Gray (Grays) sued Ford Motor Company and others.
context: Court describing the accident that caused injuries giving rise to the litigation that exposed Ford's knowledge and decisions regarding the defect.

label: Whistleblower engineer Copp testified to management knowledge
original_label: Whistleblower engineer Copp testified to management knowledge
quote: Harley Copp, a former Ford engineer and executive in charge of the crash testing program, testified that the highest level of Ford's management made the decision to go forward with the production of the Pinto, knowing that the gas tank was vulnerable to puncture and rupture at low rear impact speeds creating a significant risk of death or injury from fire and knowing that 'fixes' were feasible at nominal cost.
context: Testimony of Copp, a former Ford executive who provided first-hand evidence of management's knowledge and deliberate choice to defer safety fixes.

label: Plaintiffs' engineers tested and evaluated design alternatives
original_label: Plaintiffs' engineers tested and evaluated design alternatives
quote: Tests conducted by Ford on other vehicles, including modified or reinforced mechanical Pinto prototypes, proved safe at speeds at which the Pinto failed. Where rubber bladders had been installed in the tank, crash tests into fixed barriers at 21 miles per hour withstood leakage from punctures in the gas tank. Vehicles with fuel tanks installed above rather than behind the rear axle passed the fuel system integrity test at 31-miles-per-hour fixed barrier. A Pinto with two longitudinal hat sections added to firm up the rear structure passed a 20-mile-per-hour rear impact fixed barrier test with no fuel leakage.
context: Court documents reviewing Ford's own test data showing feasible design alternatives, used by plaintiffs' experts to prove the defect was correctable.

label: Cost of remedial design changes documented as minimal
original_label: Cost of remedial design changes documented as minimal
quote: Design changes that would have enhanced the integrity of the fuel tank system at relatively little cost per car included the following: Longitudinal side members and cross members at $2.40 and $1.80, respectively; a single shock absorbant 'flak suit' to protect the tank at $4; a tank within a tank and placement of the tank over the axle at $5.08 to $5.79; a nylon bladder within the tank at $5.25 to $8; placement of the tank over the axle surrounded with a protective barrier at a cost of $9.95 per car; substitution of a rear axle with a smooth differential housing at a cost of $2.10; imposition of a protective shield between the differential housing and the tank at $2.35; improvement and reenforcement of the bumper at $2.60; addition of eight inches of crush space a cost of $6.40.
context: Court documents itemizing the cost of feasible design alternatives, showing that safety fixes were economically viable options that Ford had rejected.

label: Engineering standard required redesign upon test failure
original_label: Engineering standard required redesign upon test failure
quote: When a prototype failed the fuel system integrity test, the standard of care for engineers in the industry was to redesign and retest it.
context: Court describing the professional engineering standard of care that Ford violated by proceeding with production despite test failures.

label: Manufacturers optimized vehicles to pass lab test, not meet real-world limits
original_label: Manufacturers optimized vehicles to pass lab test, not meet real-world limits
quote: Before September 2015 the discrepancies were generally attributed to the inadequacy of the NEDC laboratory test, which is not representative of real-world emissions, and to the optimisation strategies put in place by car manufacturers to pass the laboratory test by calibrating vehicles' ECTs so that their effectiveness is only ensured within the boundary conditions of the NEDC test.
context: The European Parliament's committee of inquiry summarizes findings on how manufacturers designed emission control systems deliberately optimized for lab conditions only.

label: Commercial choices drove optimization strategies reducing effectiveness
original_label: Commercial choices drove optimization strategies reducing effectiveness
quote: Optimisation strategies that reduce the effectiveness of ECTs can be attributed to commercial choices made by the car manufacturer to achieve different objectives, such as reducing fuel consumption, increasing user convenience, reducing costs by using cheaper parts or addressing design constraints. These objectives are not covered by the exemptions on the prohibition on the use of defeat devices.
context: The committee concludes that manufacturers' optimization strategies were economically motivated and not technically justified.

label: Volkswagen installed software to detect test conditions and reduce controls
original_label: Volkswagen installed software to detect test conditions and reduce controls
quote: After Volkswagen's admissions about the software installed in its Euro 5 EA 189 diesel engine a piece of software that enables the vehicle to recognise that it is undergoing testing and to change the NOx emission characteristic in that testing.
context: The committee describes the core misconduct: Volkswagen's explicit defeat device software.

label: Laboratory test cycle detectable and exploitable by software
original_label: Laboratory test cycle detectable and exploitable by software
quote: The NEDC, performed on a cold vehicle at 20-30 °C, consists of four repeated ECE-15 urban driving cycles (UDC), characterised by low vehicle speed, low engine load, low exhaust gas temperature and one Extra-Urban driving cycle (EUDC) to account for higher load driving conditions. It was last updated in 1997. By definition, the NEDC test cannot detect the illegal use of a defeat device.
context: The committee describes the test procedure itself as a suitable target because its predictable parameters and inability to detect cheating made it exploitable.

label: Type-approval authorities rely on manufacturer-supplied test data
original_label: Type-approval authorities rely on manufacturer-supplied test data
quote: The tests required for the type-approval procedure are often carried out in the car manufacturers' certified laboratories under the supervision of the designated technical service, often because of the lack of resources on the side of the authorities (so-called witness testing).
context: The committee identifies a structural vulnerability: regulators depend on manufacturers' own test facilities and data.

label: Consumers and fleet operators unaware of real emissions
original_label: Consumers and fleet operators unaware of real emissions
quote: There are large discrepancies between the NOx emissions of most Euro 3-6 diesel cars measured during the type-approval process with the New European Driving Cycle (NEDC) laboratory test, which meet the legal emission limit, and their NOx emissions measured in real driving conditions, which substantially exceed the limit.
context: The committee describes how vehicles appeared compliant in certified tests but exceeded limits in real use, deceiving purchasers and regulators about actual environmental and health impacts.

label: EPA detected non-compliance through unscheduled independent testing
original_label: EPA detected non-compliance through unscheduled independent testing
quote: The request by the US EPA to Volkswagen to justify the emission strategies used in their diesel cars in the US was at the origin of the admission of the use of prohibited defeat devices.
context: The committee identifies the EPA as a capable guardian that, through its demand for justification of emission strategies, forced disclosure of the defeat device.

label: JRC had technical expertise and conducted independent on-road testing
original_label: JRC had technical expertise and conducted independent on-road testing
quote: In August 2005 the Commission's Joint Research Centre (JRC) was mandated to carry out research on real driving emissions. The experimental programme of on-road tests of Euro 3 and 4 light-duty vehicles with Portable Emissions Measurement Systems (PEMS), which measure emissions from combustion engines as the vehicle is being used, allowing real-world in-use testing, started in 2007, with the first results published in 2007 and 2009, and continued with the first on-road test of a Euro 5 vehicle in June 2009.
context: The committee documents the JRC's technical capacity and early independent testing program that could have detected the discrepancies and guided regulatory action.

label: JRC concluded PEMS testing sufficiently robust by 2010
original_label: JRC concluded PEMS testing sufficiently robust by 2010
quote: The JRC also concluded that PEMS testing was able to provide accurate on-road measurement of NOx emissions in light-duty vehicles and could provide a robust tool for new regulation. The November 2010 workshop concluded that the Real Driving Emissions (RDE) test method should be ready for adoption by the end of 2012.
context: The committee shows the JRC had the technical capacity and evidence to recommend real-world testing much earlier than actually adopted.

label: Commission failed to use Regulatory Procedure with Scrutiny to escalate
original_label: Commission failed to use Regulatory Procedure with Scrutiny to escalate
quote: Despite the issue of pollutant emissions from vehicles being not only a highly sensitive and political issue, but also a subject of great concern to EU citizens, the Commission did not make any attempt to advance the decision-making process by making use of the possibility envisaged in the Regulatory Procedure with Scrutiny to bring the proposal to the level of the Council in order to increase political awareness and to exercise additional pressure on obstructing Member States. The Commission's failure to act in a timely manner on its responsibility to keep the test procedure under review and to revise it to reflect real world conditions constitutes maladministration.
context: The committee concludes the Commission possessed escalation powers but did not use them to overcome Member State obstruction of stronger testing, constituting regulatory failure.

label: Industry heavily overrepresented in RDE working group
original_label: Industry heavily overrepresented in RDE working group
quote: Over half of the RDE-LDV working group participants consisted of experts from car manufacturers and other automotive industries. This can inter alia be attributed to the lack of sufficient technical expertise in the Commission departments. While the Commission consulted a wide range of stakeholders and ensured open access to the RDE-LDV group, it should have taken further steps to 'as far as possible, ensure a balanced representation of relevant stakeholders, taking into account the specific tasks of the expert group and the type of expertise required', as required by the horizontal rules for Commission expert groups of 10 November 2010.
context: The committee documents how industry captured the regulatory process by dominating the working group due to Commission resource weakness.

label: Type-approval authorities lacked in-house testing resources and expertise
original_label: Type-approval authorities lacked in-house testing resources and expertise
quote: The presence of adequate in-house independent, qualified human resources and the availability of in-house state-of-the-art testing facilities are essential to ensuring effective monitoring of the emission standards. However, the level of technical expertise and human and financial resources may vary substantially between type-approval authorities and technical services, and the lack of a harmonised interpretation of the rules can lead to competition among them.
context: The committee identifies structural resource weakness in national regulators that left them dependent on manufacturer-controlled testing.

label: Member States did not enforce ban on defeat devices before 2015
original_label: Member States did not enforce ban on defeat devices before 2015
quote: No EU or Member State authority searched for defeat devices or proved the illegal use of defeat devices before September 2015. No Member State authority or technical service performed any tests other than the NEDC in the scope of type-approval, which in itself cannot point to the use of a defeat device.
context: The committee documents the complete absence of proactive guardianship: no enforcement activity on defeat devices despite the ban existing since 1999.

label: Technical services financed by manufacturers, creating conflicts of interest
original_label: Technical services financed by manufacturers, creating conflicts of interest
quote: The fact that type-approval authorities and technical services are usually financed in part by fees paid directly to them by the car manufacturers can give rise to conflicts of interest due to the need to maintain commercial relations. Moreover, some technical services also do consultancy work for manufacturers on emission tests.
context: The committee identifies structural conflicts of interest: the guardians depended financially on those they were supposed to regulate.

label: Commission did not request information despite indications of defeat devices
original_label: Commission did not request information despite indications of defeat devices
quote: The Commission had no legal obligation to search for defeat devices itself, but had the legal obligation to oversee the Member States' enforcement of the ban on defeat devices. However, in spite of the awareness of, and communication between the relevant Commission services on, possible illegal practices by manufacturers contravening Regulation (EC) No 715/2007, the Commission neither undertook any further technical or legal research or investigation, either on its own or by mandating the JRC, nor requested any information or further action from the Member States to verify whether the law may have been infringed. This constitutes maladministration and a failure to act.
context: The committee concludes the Commission knew of concerning evidence but failed to investigate or demand investigation, constituting a breakdown in oversight.

label: Member States delayed RDE adoption to favor higher conformity factors
original_label: Member States delayed RDE adoption to favor higher conformity factors
quote: The analysis of the minutes of the RDE-LDV working group and of the TCMV shows that some Member States acted on several occasions to delay the adoption process of the RDE tests and to favour less stringent testing methods. In addition, several Member States (Italy, Spain, France, the Slovak Republic, Romania and Hungary) prevented the formation of a qualified majority in the TCMV, resulting in a postponement of the vote on the first RDE package, and therefore a delay in the whole RDE process.
context: The committee documents how Member States captured the regulatory process by blocking stricter testing to protect their automotive industries.

label: Commission did not escalate JRC evidence of concerning emissions behavior
original_label: Commission did not escalate JRC evidence of concerning emissions behavior
quote: On 30 April 2012 an internal e-mail from the JRC, with DG GROW in copy, was sent on the subject of a Euro 5a diesel passenger vehicle that was being tested by the JRC. The test results showed that the Euro 5 emission limits were only fulfilled in the temperature range between 20 and 30 °C, but were not met outside of that temperature window. The e-mail also mentions a 'memory effect' that was found to influence the engine strategy for at least 20 minutes after starting the engine at a specific temperature. The official in DG GROW who replied to the email, with DG ENV and DG MOVE in copy, stated that 'this is very useful and a clear case of hard cycle beating'. In their hearing before the committee, the then Director and Director-General of DG GROW stated that they were not informed about this e-mail and therefore no follow-up action was taken.
context: The committee documents how JRC evidence of suspicious emissions behavior (thermal windows, memory effects) was documented in internal emails but never escalated or investigated.

label: Manufacturers exploited narrow temperature range of NEDC test
original_label: Manufacturers exploited narrow temperature range of NEDC test
quote: Some manufacturers decrease the effectiveness of ECTs outside specific 'thermal windows' that are close to the ambient temperature range prescribed by the NEDC, for instance by switching off emission control systems at ambient temperatures below 17 °C, while others are able to keep ECTs effective in much larger temperature ranges. Those thermal windows are rarely justifiable according to the technical limitations of the ECTs.
context: The committee documents how manufacturers designed defeat strategies around the predictable test parameters: the narrow temperature window of the NEDC.

label: Manufacturers modulate controls after approximately 20 minutes of test duration
original_label: Manufacturers modulate controls after approximately 20 minutes of test duration
quote: One example is stopping or modulating ECTs to decrease their efficiency after a certain time from the start of the engine, close to the duration of the test (approximately 20 minutes), has elapsed.
context: The committee identifies how manufacturers designed defeat strategies to expire at the known end of the NEDC test duration.

label: Type-approval authorities certified vehicles without running additional tests
original_label: Type-approval authorities certified vehicles without running additional tests
quote: Before the Volkswagen revelations in September 2015, despite evidence of significant exceedances of on-road NOx emissions compared to the regulatory limits made available by the Commission and other independent bodies, and despite the ban on defeat devices enshrined in EU law, no Member State applied specific protocols or test methods, or took any other measure, to search for the possible use of prohibited defeat devices. Several type-approval authorities and technical services also mentioned the lack of a test method to identify defeat devices.
context: The committee shows manufacturers exploited the predictable routine that regulators would approve vehicles based only on the standard NEDC test, without supplementary testing.

label: Commission DG ENV requested enforcement but was overruled
original_label: Commission DG ENV requested enforcement but was overruled
quote: The Commission's DG ENV asked for better enforcement of the Euro 3/4/5 emission standards as regards the existing fleet. However, the proposal by the then Commissioner Potočnik to the then Commissioner Tajani to examine policy options with respect to the current fleet was not taken on board by the latter, on the grounds that no legal action was considered possible towards cars that complied with the existing testing protocols under the current legislation.
context: The committee documents an internal handler (DG ENV) attempting to enforce the law but being overruled by a superior (Commissioner Tajani responsible for industry).

label: JRC internal notes characterized emission behavior as hard cycle beating
original_label: JRC internal notes characterized emission behavior as hard cycle beating
quote: The official in DG GROW who replied to the email, with DG ENV and DG MOVE in copy, stated that 'this is very useful and a clear case of hard cycle beating'.
context: An internal Commission handler (DG GROW official) recognized the suspicious behavior and labeled it appropriately, but took no action.

label: No comprehensive internal control for defeat device compliance before 2015
original_label: No comprehensive internal control for defeat device compliance before 2015
quote: Unlike in the case of heavy-duty vehicles, car manufacturers were not required to disclose or justify their emission strategies. Having such an obligation would facilitate controlling for defeat devices.
context: The committee notes the absence of a basic internal control mechanism: manufacturers had no obligation to disclose or justify their emission control strategies.

category: Legitimate access and separation from victims
label: Manufacturers occupy legitimate positions on type-approval authorities expert groups
original_label: Manufacturers occupy legitimate positions on type-approval authorities expert groups
quote: In three group meetings that took place between May and September 2016 with 43 to 47 participants, 21-23 represented car manufacturers, 9-12 other automotive industry actors, 5-7 Member States, 1-5 technical services, and 1-2 research institutes, civil society or NGOs.
context: The committee documents how manufacturers had legitimate access to the regulatory process through their majority presence in the RDE working group.

category: Legitimate access and separation from victims
label: Manufacturers choose which type-approval authority to approach
original_label: Manufacturers choose which type-approval authority to approach
quote: Under the current legislation – and the EU single market rules – type-approval granted in a Member State is recognised throughout the Union. Although common rules on type-approval and test specifications are laid down, many witnesses highlighted the existence of a variety of interpretations in their application across the Member States. While in many cases the choice by a car manufacturer of the type-approval authority of a certain Member State is due to geographical or historical reasons, the lack of a harmonised interpretation of the rules can lead to a situation of competition among the type-approval authorities of different Member States, as car manufacturers may choose an authority on the basis of its flexibility in the interpretation of the rules.
context: The committee describes how manufacturers had legitimate control over which regulator to approach, enabling them to select the most lenient or flexible authority.

category: Legitimate access and separation from victims
label: Manufacturers choose and contract technical services directly
original_label: Manufacturers choose and contract technical services directly
quote: It is the car manufacturer that usually chooses the technical service to be used: in principle, the type-approval authority can challenge the choice, but it seldom does so. National authorities have never asked technical services to perform additional tests to ensure the implementation of the requirement to meet the regulatory limit in 'normal use' or of the ban on defeat devices. For technical services, running additional tests on their own initiative would entail supplementary costs and might put their commercial relationships with manufacturers at risk.
context: The committee shows manufacturers controlled who tested their vehicles and could avoid additional scrutiny by selecting compliant service providers.

category: Legitimate access and separation from victims
label: Manufacturers spatially separated from regulatory testing oversight
original_label: Manufacturers spatially separated from regulatory testing oversight
quote: The Member States should have ensured that their type-approval authorities have sufficient human and financial resources to perform in-house testing. They should have not relied on tests performed in the car manufacturers' certified laboratories under the supervision of technical services.
context: The committee identifies spatial separation: testing occurred in manufacturer facilities under limited regulatory supervision, giving manufacturers control over the testing environment.

label: Thermal windows justified as engine protection despite technical weakness
original_label: Thermal windows justified as engine protection despite technical weakness
quote: Some manufacturers decrease the effectiveness of ECTs outside specific 'thermal windows' close to the temperature range prescribed by the NEDC test, claiming that such a decrease is necessary to protect the engine against damage in line with the derogations to the ban on defeat devices provided for in Article 5(2) of Regulation (EC) No 715/2007. Those thermal windows are rarely justifiable according to the technical limitations of the ECTs.
context: The committee documents how manufacturers deployed a legal-appearing justification (engine protection exception) that concealed the actual technical reality and was rarely technically sound.

label: All manufacturers claimed use of defeat device exceptions without justification
original_label: All manufacturers claimed use of defeat device exceptions without justification
quote: The vast majority of car manufacturers present on the EU market declared that they use the derogations to the ban on defeat devices provided for in Article 5(2) of Regulation (EC) No 715/2007.
context: The committee shows manufacturers used legal language to claim compliance while actually implementing prohibited strategies.

label: Manufacturers interpreted laboratory compliance as only legal requirement
original_label: Manufacturers interpreted laboratory compliance as only legal requirement
quote: In their written answers and during the hearings, Member States and car manufacturers stated that they interpreted the legislation in such a way that the NEDC test in the laboratory was the only requirement for vehicles to pass, despite the air-quality objectives of the legislation.
context: The committee documents how manufacturers and regulators adopted a narrow, technically compliant but legally evasive interpretation that the lab test was the only requirement.

label: Commission and JRC did not escalate findings to political level
original_label: Commission and JRC did not escalate findings to political level
quote: The Commission should have ensured that the JRC's research findings and concerns discussed among the Commission services with regard to possible illegal practices by manufacturers reached the higher levels of the hierarchy – which allegedly did not happen – so that appropriate action could be taken.
context: The committee notes evidence of illegal practices remained at technical staff levels without escalation to political decision-makers, maintaining surface appearance of compliance.

label: West Virginia University study found VW emissions 35 times EPA standard
original_label: West Virginia University study found VW emissions 35 times EPA standard
quote: 15 May A study conducted by the Center for Alternative Fuels, Engines and Emissions at West Virginia University for the International Council on Clean Transportation (ICCT) finds that real world nitrogen oxide (NOx) emissions from two tested Volkswagen (VW) light-duty diesel vehicles exceeds US Environment Protection Agency (EPA) standards by a factor of up to 35.
context: The timeline documents the first independent detection: unscheduled academic testing by researchers outside the regulatory framework.

label: EPA investigation escalated and Volkswagen admitted defeat device use
original_label: EPA investigation escalated and Volkswagen admitted defeat device use
quote: 3 September Executives from VW admit in a private call to EPA the existence of defeat device software that served to understate NOx emissions in official tests and circumvent EPA emissions standards; 18 September The EPA issues a Notice of Violation of the Clean Air Act to Volkswagen AG.
context: The timeline marks the convergence break: EPA initiated investigation, forcing VW admission, leading to formal violation notice.

label: EPA requested VW justify emission strategies, forcing defeat device disclosure
original_label: EPA requested VW justify emission strategies, forcing defeat device disclosure
quote: The request by the US EPA to Volkswagen to justify the emission strategies used in their diesel cars in the US was at the origin of the admission of the use of prohibited defeat devices.
context: The committee explains the specific mechanism of detection: EPA's demand for manufacturers to justify their strategies forced disclosure.

label: National investigations launched after September 2015 Volkswagen revelation
original_label: National investigations launched after September 2015 Volkswagen revelation
quote: The Member States started to enforce the EU law on emissions from light-duty vehicles as required only after the Volkswagen emissions case broke in September 2015, by conducting additional tests in the laboratory and on the road, and by launching several national investigations into pollutant emissions from passenger cars.
context: The committee documents how detection of Volkswagen's fraud triggered immediate behavioral change: Member States began enforcing law and running tests for the first time.

label: Commission initiated infringement procedures after evidence gathered

original_label: Pilot training dependent on FAA certification determinations

In connection with the overall evaluation, approval and certification process for a derivative airplane, the FAA-AEG is responsible for determining the required level of differences training for U.S.-based airline pilots – and, relatedly, the extent to which new or updated functions must be described in the flight manuals – based on information provided, and recommendations made, by manufacturers such as Boeing.
