label: FAA certification procedures require safety assessment
original_label: FAA certification procedures require safety assessment
quote: The FAA's procedures for aircraft type certification require an aircraft manufacturer ("applicant") to demonstrate that its design complies with all applicable FAA regulations and requirements. For transport-category airplanes, as part of this process, applicants must demonstrate through analysis, test, or both that their design meets the applicable requirements under Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations (CFR) Part 25.
context: NTSB description of FAA's formal mandate and procedures for overseeing aircraft design certification.

label: FAA guidance on flight crew alerting and system design
original_label: FAA guidance on flight crew alerting and system design
quote: Title 14 CFR 25.1322 addresses flight crew alerting and states, in part, that flight crew alerts must (1) Provide the flightcrew with the information needed to: (i) Identify non-normal operation or airplane system conditions, and (ii) Determine the appropriate actions, if any. (2) Be readily and easily detectable and intelligible by the flightcrew under all foreseeable operating conditions, including conditions where multiple alerts are provided.
context: NTSB citation of FAA regulatory standards that were in effect to guide design oversight.

label: Manufacturer assumptions accepted without comprehensive validation
original_label: Manufacturer assumptions accepted without comprehensive validation
quote: Boeing indicated to the NTSB that, based on FAA guidance, it used assumptions during its safety assessment of MCAS hazards in the engineering flight simulator. Four of these assumptions were the following: Uncommanded system inputs are readily recognizable and can be counteracted by overriding the failure by movement of the flight controls "in the normal sense" by the flight crew and do not require specific procedures. Action to counter the failure shall not require exceptional piloting skill or strength. The pilot will take immediate action to reduce or eliminate increased control forces by re-trimming or changing configuration or flight conditions. Trained flight crew memory procedures shall be followed to address and eliminate or mitigate the failure.
context: NTSB finding that FAA guidance permitted manufacturers to make broad assumptions about pilot response without requiring comprehensive testing of those assumptions.

label: Safety assessment did not evaluate combined alert effects
original_label: Safety assessment did not evaluate combined alert effects
quote: While Boeing considered the possibility of uncommanded MCAS operation as part of its functional hazard assessment, it did not evaluate all the potential alerts and indications that could accompany a failure that also resulted in uncommanded MCAS operation. Therefore, neither Boeing's system safety assessment nor its simulator tests evaluated how the combined effect of alerts and indications might impact pilots' recognition of which procedure(s) to prioritize in responding to an unintended MCAS operation caused by an erroneous AOA input.
context: NTSB analysis identifying the gap in Boeing's assessment process that FAA oversight failed to catch or require closure of.

label: FAA guidance lacks methods for evaluating pilot error probability
original_label: FAA guidance lacks methods for evaluating pilot error probability
quote: As early as 2002, the joint FAA-industry study recognized that, while excellent guidance existed for manufacturers on various topics salient to the development of system safety assessments, there were no methods available to evaluate the probability of human error in the operation of a particular system design and that existing qualitative methods for assessing human error were not "very satisfactory." The 2002 study went on to state that the processes used to determine and validate human responses to failure and methods to include human responses in safety assessments needed to be improved.
context: NTSB analysis showing that FAA oversight framework lacked the tools or standards to require robust pilot performance validation.

label: Regulatory guidance unchanged for 31 years despite known gaps
original_label: Regulatory guidance unchanged for 31 years despite known gaps
quote: The NTSB notes that a number of human performance research studies have been conducted in the years since the certification guidance contained in AC 25.1309-1A was put in place (in 1988) and this study was conducted and it is likely that more rigorous, validated methodologies exist today to assess error tolerance with regard to pilot recognition and response to failure conditions. The NTSB also believes that the use of validated methods and tools to assess pilot performance in dealing with failure conditions and emergencies would result in more effective requirements for flight deck interface design, pilot procedures, and training strategies. However, we are concerned that such tools and methods are still not commonplace or required as part of the design certification process for functions such as MCAS on newly certified type designs.
context: NTSB observation that despite 31 years of research and known methodological gaps, FAA had not updated guidance to require stronger pilot performance validation.

label: Simulator test of MCAS isolated from failure context
original_label: Simulator test of MCAS isolated from failure context
quote: To perform these simulator tests, Boeing induced a stabilizer trim input that would simulate the stabilizer moving at a rate and duration consistent with the MCAS function. Using this method to induce the hazard resulted in the following: motion of the stabilizer trim wheel, increased column forces, and indication that the airplane was moving nose down. Boeing indicated to the NTSB that this evaluation was focused on the pilot response to uncommanded MCAS operation, regardless of underlying cause. Thus, the specific failure modes that could lead to uncommanded MCAS activation (such as an erroneous high AOA input to the MCAS) were not simulated as part of these functional hazard assessment validation tests.
context: NTSB finding that Boeing's simulator protocol, following standard FAA guidance, only tested isolated system failure rather than the complete failure scenario that pilots would encounter.

label: Functional hazard assessment process follows standardized categories
original_label: Functional hazard assessment process follows standardized categories
quote: For the normal flight envelope, Boeing identified and classified two hazards associated with "uncommanded MCAS" activation as "major." One of these hazards, applicable to the MCAS function seen in these accidents, included uncommanded MCAS operation to maximum authority. Boeing indicated that, as part of the functional hazard assessment development, pilot assessments of MCAS-related hazards were conducted in an engineering flight simulator, including the uncommanded MCAS operation (stabilizer runaway) to the MCAS maximum authority.
context: NTSB description of how Boeing applied the routine FAA hazard classification process to MCAS.

label: Boeing conducted safety assessments per guidance
original_label: Boeing conducted safety assessments per guidance
quote: As part of demonstrating 737 MAX 8 compliance with the requirements in 14 CFR 25.1309, Boeing conducted a number of airplane- and system-level safety assessments, consistent with the guidance provided in AC 25.1309-1A.
context: NTSB factual finding that Boeing internal processes included required safety assessment steps according to regulation.

label: Boeing simulator evaluation of MCAS was Boeing-designed process
original_label: Boeing simulator evaluation of MCAS was Boeing-designed process
quote: Boeing indicated that this evaluation was focused on the pilot response to uncommanded MCAS operation, regardless of underlying cause.
context: NTSB noting that Boeing designed its own validation methodology for MCAS rather than independently validating it.

category: Legitimate access and separation from victims
label: Boeing occupational role as designer submitting for certification
original_label: Boeing occupational role as designer submitting for certification
quote: As the development of the 737 MAX progressed, the MCAS function was expanded to low Mach numbers. As originally delivered, the MCAS became active during manual flight (autopilot not engaged) when the flaps were fully retracted and the airplane's AOA value (as measured by either AOA sensor) exceeded a threshold based on Mach number.
context: NTSB factual description of Boeing's legitimate design authority and how MCAS was integrated into aircraft.

category: Legitimate access and separation from victims
label: Boeing provided safety assessment to FAA for review and approval
original_label: Boeing provided safety assessment to FAA for review and approval
quote: Safety assessments are performed by the manufacturer and its suppliers and are reviewed and accepted by the FAA.
context: NTSB footnote explaining that Boeing's assessment of MCAS was submitted through legitimate regulatory channels.

category: Legitimate access and separation from victims
label: Pilots spatially and temporally distant from design decisions
original_label: Pilots spatially and temporally distant from design decisions
quote: Multiple alerts and indications can increase pilots' workload and can also make it more difficult to identify which procedure the pilots should conduct. The NTSB notes that the Lion Air and Ethiopian Airlines accident pilots' responses to multiple alerts and indications are similar to the circumstances of a 2009 accident involving Air France flight 447, an Airbus A330, which was traveling from Rio de Janeiro to Paris when it crashed in the Atlantic Ocean.
context: NTSB analysis showing pilots were operationally separated from the design and certification process that created the hazard they faced.

label: MCAS described in terms that minimize its significance
original_label: MCAS described in terms that minimize its significance
quote: Boeing implemented aerodynamic changes as well as a stability augmentation function, MCAS, as an extension of the existing speed trim system to improve aircraft handling characteristics and decrease pitch-up tendency at elevated AOA.
context: NTSB description of how Boeing characterized MCAS as a minor extension of existing systems rather than a novel flight control system requiring independent validation.

label: Boeing conclusions stated without noting test limitations
original_label: Boeing conclusions stated without noting test limitations
quote: In a 2019 presentation to the NTSB, Boeing indicated that the MCAS hazard classification of "major" for uncommanded MCAS function in the normal flight envelope was based on the following conclusions: Unintended stabilizer trim inputs are readily recognized by movement of the stabilizer trim wheel, flightpath change, or increased column forces. Aircraft can be returned to steady level flight using available column (elevator) alone or stabilizer trim. Continuous unintended nose-down stabilizer trim inputs would be recognized as a stabilizer trim or stabilizer runaway failure and the procedure for stabilizer runaway would be followed.
context: NTSB finding that Boeing presented safety conclusions to the NTSB without disclosing that these conclusions were based on isolated simulator tests that did not include the full failure scenario.

label: First accident revealed operational failure of MCAS system
original_label: First accident revealed operational failure of MCAS system
quote: On October 29, 2018, Lion Air flight 610, a Boeing 737 MAX 8, PK-LQP, crashed in the Java Sea shortly after takeoff from Soekarno-Hatta International Airport, Jakarta, Indonesia. The flight crew had communicated with air traffic control and indicated that they were having flight control and altitude issues before the airplane disappeared from radar. The flight was a scheduled domestic flight from Jakarta to Depati Amir Airport, Pangkal Pinang City, Bangka Belitung Islands Province, Indonesia. All 189 passengers and crew on board died, and the airplane was destroyed.
context: NTSB accident narrative describing the first crash that exposed MCAS failure and prompted investigation.

label: Second accident repeated MCAS failure pattern
original_label: Second accident repeated MCAS failure pattern
quote: On March 10, 2019, Ethiopian Airlines flight 302, a Boeing 737 MAX 8, Ethiopian registration ET-AVJ, crashed near Ejere, Ethiopia, shortly after takeoff from Addis Ababa Bole International Airport, Ethiopia. The flight was a scheduled international passenger flight from Addis Ababa to Jomo Kenyatta International Airport, Nairobi, Kenya. All 157 passengers and crew on board died, and the airplane was destroyed.
context: NTSB accident narrative describing the second crash that confirmed the MCAS system design flaw and triggered safety investigation.

label: DFDR data revealed erroneous AOA sensor inputs in accidents
original_label: DFDR data revealed erroneous AOA sensor inputs in accidents

During rotation, the left (captain's) stick shaker activated, and DFDR data showed that the left airspeed and altitude values disagreed with, and were lower than, the corresponding values from the right.

label: Investigation compared design assumptions to actual pilot behavior
original_label: Investigation compared design assumptions to actual pilot behavior
quote: we are concerned that the accident pilot responses to the unintended MCAS operation were not consistent with the underlying assumptions about pilot recognition and response that Boeing used, based on FAA guidance, for flight control system functional hazard assessments, including for MCAS, as part of the 737 MAX design.

label: NTSB investigation examined design certification process
original_label: NTSB investigation examined design certification process
quote: As the accident investigation authority for the state of design and manufacture of the airplane in these accidents, the NTSB has been examining the US design certification process used to approve the original design of the Maneuvering Characteristics Augmentation System (MCAS) on the Boeing Company (Boeing) 737 MAX.

label: FAA guidance requirements for pilot recognition of failures
original_label: FAA guidance requirements for pilot recognition of failures
quote: AC 25-7C stated that short-term forces are the initial stabilized control forces that result from maintaining the intended flightpath after configuration changes and normal transitions from one flight condition to another, "or from regaining control following a failure. It is assumed that the pilot will take immediate action to reduce or eliminate such forces by re-trimming or changing configuration or flight conditions, and consequently short-term forces are not considered to exist for any significant duration [emphasis added]."

label: Pilot assumptions standardized across all Boeing models
original_label: Pilot assumptions standardized across all Boeing models

label: FAA permitted assumptions without requiring comprehensive testing
original_label: FAA permitted assumptions without requiring comprehensive testing
quote: Consistent with this philosophy, the NTSB notes that FAA certification guidance in AC 25.1309-1A that allows manufacturers to assume pilots will respond to failure conditions appropriately is based, in part, upon the applicant showing that the systems, controls, and associated monitoring and warnings are designed to minimize crew errors, which could create additional hazards.
context: NTSB analysis identifying how FAA guidance structure permitted Boeing to make untested assumptions about pilot performance.

label: Hazard classification drove downstream safety requirements
original_label: Hazard classification drove downstream safety requirements

Boeing was then required to verify that each system that supported MCAS complied with the quantitative and qualitative safety requirements for a "major" hazard, as provided in AC 25.1309-1A, and demonstrate this to the FAA in its aircraft and system safety assessments.

label: No comprehensive data requirement for multiple alert scenarios
original_label: No comprehensive data requirement for multiple alert scenarios
quote: if manufacturers assume correct pilot response without comprehensively examining all possible flight deck alerts and indications that may occur for system and component failures that contribute to a given hazard, the hazard classification and resulting system design (including alerts and indications), procedural, and/or training mitigations may not adequately consider and account for the potential for pilots to take actions that are inconsistent with manufacturer assumptions.

label: Previous flight before accident showed same erroneous AOA input
original_label: Previous flight before accident showed same erroneous AOA input

label: Boeing classified MCAS hazard as acceptable risk level
original_label: Boeing classified MCAS hazard as acceptable risk level

original_label: Board exercises operational control as executives

quote: An FDA scientist who evaluated OxyContin wrote in his original review: 'Care should be taken to limit competitive promotion.' The Sacklers did not agree. From the beginning, the Sacklers viewed limits on opioids as an obstacle to greater profits.
context: Complaint identifies the FDA as a guardian with authority over drug approval and marketing, noting the regulator's caution about aggressive promotion.

label: DEA tracking of opioid distribution and diversion
original_label: DEA tracking of opioid distribution and diversion
quote: That spring, Purdue executives met with the U.S. Drug Enforcement Agency ('DEA'). A senior DEA official sat across from Richard Sackler. Before the meeting ended, she leaned over the table and told Richard: 'People are dying. Do you understand that?'
context: Complaint describes the DEA as a potential guardian that engaged with Purdue leadership, expressing concern about opioid-related deaths.

label: State attorneys general as enforcement guardians
original_label: State attorneys general as enforcement guardians
quote: As Purdue kept pushing opioids and people kept dying, the company was engulfed in a wave of investigations by state attorneys general, the DEA, and the U.S. Department of Justice.
context: Complaint indicates that state attorneys general and federal agencies were investigating Purdue's opioid marketing practices.

label: 2007 guilty plea and corporate integrity agreement not preventing recurrence
original_label: 2007 guilty plea and corporate integrity agreement not preventing recurrence
quote: By 2006, prosecutors found damning evidence that Purdue intentionally deceived doctors and patients about its opioids. The Sacklers voted that their first drug company, the Purdue Frederick Company, should plead guilty to a felony for misbranding OxyContin as less addictive, less subject to abuse and diversion, and less likely to cause adverse events and side effects than other pain medications. In May 2007, the Sacklers voted again to have their company plead guilty and enter a series of agreements that Purdue would never deceive doctors and patients about opioids again.
context: Complaint describes prior criminal conviction and corporate integrity agreements that failed to prevent continued misconduct, showing weakness in guardianship enforcement mechanisms.

label: Purdue's own compliance function inadequate to detect diversion
original_label: Purdue's own compliance function inadequate to detect diversion
quote: Staff reported to the Sacklers that they received 572 Reports of Concern about abuse and diversion of Purdue opioids during Q2 2007 — including several reports in Massachusetts. Staff reported that they completed only 21 field inquiries in response. Staff also told the Sacklers that they received more than 100 calls to Purdue's compliance hotline during the quarter, which was a 'significant increase,' but Purdue did not report any of the hotline calls or Reports of Concern to the FDA, DEA, Department of Justice, or state authorities.
context: Complaint shows that Purdue's internal compliance system received hundreds of reports of problematic prescribing but failed to investigate or report them, weakening external guardianship.

label: Non-reporting of Region Zero suspicious prescribers
original_label: Non-reporting of Region Zero suspicious prescribers
quote: The 2007 Judgment further required that Purdue establish and follow an abuse and diversion detection program to identify high-prescribing doctors who show signs of inappropriate prescribing, stop promoting drugs to them, and report them to the authorities. Staff reported to the Sacklers that if Region Zero doctors stopped prescribing opioids, Purdue would lose almost 10% of its sales. In response to the Board's request, staff reported to the Board that Purdue suspected Dr. Michael Taylor, in New Bedford, Massachusetts, was prescribing opioids inappropriately. Staff reported that, in the past two years, Taylor had prescribed OxyContin more than five hundred times, and provided Purdue with $392,505.
context: Complaint describes how Purdue tracked suspicious prescribers but continued profiting from them rather than reporting to authorities as required by consent judgment, demonstrating captured guardianship.

label: Lobbying to defeat Massachusetts restrictions on OxyContin
original_label: Lobbying to defeat Massachusetts restrictions on OxyContin
quote: Staff told the Sacklers that Purdue defeated legislation to restrict OxyContin in Massachusetts. Staff also told the Sacklers that Purdue was targeting Massachusetts prescribers with opioid savings cards: 'Emails targeted towards HCPs practicing in Massachusetts were also developed to remind them that the use of patient savings cards are now permissible in Massachusetts and that they can download OxyContin Savings Cards at PurdueHCP.com.'
context: Complaint describes Purdue's lobbying efforts to defeat legislative restrictions in Massachusetts, showing how the offender influenced the regulatory environment.

label: Insurance companies and managed care organizations influenced by Purdue
original_label: Insurance companies and managed care organizations influenced by Purdue
quote: In 2013, Purdue also increased its targeting of managed care organizations and insurance companies, including Medicaid and Medicare plans. In June and July, Paulo Costa strategized with Purdue staff, including Sales VP Russell Gasdia, to market Purdue opioids directly to insurance companies and managed care formularies. Under the plan, Purdue would try to convince them to cover opioids with data that the FDA had never approved.
context: Complaint describes how Purdue targeted insurance gatekeepers with deceptive data to influence coverage decisions, weakening their capacity to protect patients.

label: Compliance hotline calls not reported to external authorities
original_label: Compliance hotline calls not reported to external authorities
quote: Staff also told the Sacklers that they received more than 100 calls to Purdue's compliance hotline during the quarter, which was a 'significant increase,' but Purdue did not report any of the hotline calls or Reports of Concern to the FDA, DEA, Department of Justice, or state authorities.
context: Complaint shows that Purdue exploited routine compliance procedures by receiving reports but failing to escalate them to external guardians as required.

category: Legitimate access and separation from victims
label: Sales reps' legitimate access through prescriber relationships
original_label: Sales reps' legitimate access through prescriber relationships
quote: Purdue's most powerful tool of deception was sending sales representatives to promote opioids to Massachusetts doctors, nurses, and pharmacists face to face. During sales visits, Purdue reps made false and misleading claims directly to the professionals who care for Massachusetts patients. Purdue assigned reps to specific territories in Massachusetts and gave them lists of Massachusetts doctors to visit. Purdue targeted doctors, nurses, and pharmacists in every part of our Commonwealth.
context: Complaint describes how Purdue gained legitimate access to medical professionals through routine sales calls, from which position they delivered deceptive claims.

category: Legitimate access and separation from victims
label: Face-to-face sales visits without witnesses or documentation
original_label: Face-to-face sales visits without witnesses or documentation
quote: Purdue used face-to-face sales visits to conceal its deception by trying to avoid witnesses or a paper trail. When one sales rep made the mistake of writing down in an email her sales pitch to a doctor, Purdue's Vice President of Sales Russell Gasdia ordered: 'Fire her now!' Purdue's leaders did not want a record of their behavior because they knew they were breaking the law.
context: Complaint describes how Purdue leveraged the routine nature of sales visits to avoid documentation and oversight, and punished representatives who created records.

category: Legitimate access and separation from victims
label: Spatial separation between Purdue and harmed patients
original_label: Spatial separation between Purdue and harmed patients
quote: Purdue sales reps visited Massachusetts prescribers more than 150,000 times. A list of the exact date, location, sales rep, and 'target' of each sales visit is attached as Exhibit 1. Each of these in-person sales visits cost Purdue money — on average more than $200 per visit. But Purdue made that money back many times over, because it convinced doctors to prescribe its addictive drugs.
context: Complaint describes the routine business activity of sales visits through which Purdue influenced prescribing decisions, with harm occurring through prescriber intermediaries rather than direct contact.

label: False claims about addiction risk in FDA-approved materials
original_label: False claims about addiction risk in FDA-approved materials
quote: In a pamphlet for doctors, Providing Relief, Preventing Abuse: A Reference Guide To Controlled Substance Prescribing Practices, Purdue wrote that addiction 'is not caused by drugs.' Instead, Purdue assured doctors that addiction happens when the wrong patients get drugs and abuse them: 'it is triggered in a susceptible individual by exposure to drugs, most commonly through abuse.' Purdue promoted its opioids to Massachusetts patients with marketing that was designed to obscure the risk of addiction and even the fact that Purdue was behind the campaign.
context: Complaint describes how Purdue created published materials that bore apparent legitimacy as educational references while conveying systematically false information about addiction.

label: False pseudoaddiction doctrine in sponsored publications
original_label: False pseudoaddiction doctrine in sponsored publications
quote: A Purdue pamphlet titled Clinical Issues in Opioid Prescribing urged doctors to look for pseudoaddiction: 'A term which has been used to describe patient behaviors that may occur when pain is undertreated. Patients with unrelieved pain may become focused on obtaining medications, may 'clock watch,' and may otherwise seem inappropriately 'drug-seeking.' Even such behaviors as illicit drug use and deception can occur in the patient's efforts to obtain relief. Pseudoaddiction can be distinguished from true addiction in that the behaviors resolve when the pain is effectively treated.' Purdue again urged doctors to prescribe higher doses, stating that opioids 'are frequently underdosed - or even withheld due to a widespread lack of information ... about their use among healthcare professionals.'
context: Complaint describes how Purdue created medical literature that reframed addiction symptoms as evidence of inadequate dosing, providing apparent clinical justification for harmful prescribing.

label: Opioid savings cards designed to look like patient assistance
original_label: Opioid savings cards designed to look like patient assistance
quote: One of Purdue's most powerful tactics to keep patients on opioids longer was an opioid savings card that gave patients discounts on their first prescriptions. Discounts could have cut Purdue's revenue if patients took opioids for a short time. But Purdue's internal 10-year plan highlighted its discovery that opioid savings cards kept patients on opioids longer: 'more patients remain on OxyContin after 90 days.' Purdue determined that opioid savings cards worked like the teaser rate on a long-term and very high-stakes mortgage. According to Purdue's internal analysis, the savings cards had the highest 'return on investment' in the entire 'OxyContin Marketing Mix.'
context: Complaint describes how Purdue designed programs that appeared to be patient assistance but were engineered specifically to extend opioid dependence and increase company revenue.

label: Educational programs at Massachusetts medical institutions funded by Purdue
original_label: Educational programs at Massachusetts medical institutions funded by Purdue
quote: In 2009, the Sacklers decided to renew Purdue's commitment to spend $3,000,000 in Massachusetts to fund the Massachusetts General Hospital Purdue Pharma Pain Program. The Sacklers had chosen to launch the Massachusetts General Hospital Purdue Pharma Pain Program in 2002 after due diligence, including review of OxyContin sales data, led staff to conclude that it would help Purdue sell more opioids in Massachusetts.
context: Complaint describes how Purdue used educational partnerships at prestigious institutions to gain legitimacy and influence while serving its commercial interests.

label: Tufts University program funded and influenced by Sacklers
original_label: Tufts University program funded and influenced by Sacklers
quote: In 1980, three Sackler brothers, through a very large payment, established the Sackler School of Graduate Biomedical Sciences. Later, in 1999, the Sackler family made a more targeted gift, establishing Tufts Masters of Science in Pain Research, Education, and Policy ('MSPREP Program'). Kathe Sackler co-presided over the decision to fund the MSPREP Program. Richard Sackler attended the launch symposium in Boston and paid Tufts hundreds of thousands of dollars. Purdue also sponsored the annual Sackler Lecture at Tufts on a topic in pain medicine. For many years, Richard took a seat on the board of the Tufts University School of Medicine.
context: Complaint describes how the Sackler family used major philanthropic investments to gain influence over academic programs and control the direction of pain medicine education.

label: McKinsey consulting legitimizes aggressive sales tactics
original_label: McKinsey consulting legitimizes aggressive sales tactics
quote: McKinsey estimated that new tactics by Purdue sales reps would generate $200,000,000 to $400,000,000 more sales of OxyContin, and that sales reps had been practicing the new tactics in front of management. McKinsey had reported to Purdue on opportunities to increase prescriptions by convincing doctors that opioids provide 'freedom' and 'peace of mind' and give patients 'the best possible chance to live a full and active life.' McKinsey also suggested sales 'drivers' based on the ideas that opioids reduce stress and make patients more optimistic and less isolated. In fact, becoming addicted to opioids makes patients more stressed, more isolated, and less likely to survive.
context: Complaint describes how Purdue engaged prestigious consulting firms that gave professional legitimacy to sales tactics while making systematically false claims about opioid effects.

label: Abuse-deterrent reformulation marketed as safety improvement
original_label: Abuse-deterrent reformulation marketed as safety improvement
quote: By 2008, Purdue was working on a crush-proof reformulation of OxyContin to extend Purdue's patent monopoly. Mortimer Sackler suggested that Purdue conduct similar studies to find out whether reformulated OxyContin was really safer before selling it to millions of patients. He wrote to Richard Sackler: 'Purdue should be leading the charge on this type of research and should be generating the research to support our formulation. Why are we playing catch up ...? Shouldn't we have studies like this ...?' The Sacklers decided not to do the research because they wanted the profits from a new product, regardless of whether the deaths continued.
context: Complaint describes how Purdue decided to market a reformulation without conducting safety studies, allowing it to present technical modifications as safety improvements.

label: Falsely marketing abuse-deterrent properties despite FDA warning
original_label: Falsely marketing abuse-deterrent properties despite FDA warning
quote: Purdue also steered patients away from safer alternatives with false claims that its opioids had less risk of abuse. As more people died of addiction and overdose, Purdue created tamper-resistant versions of its drugs to be harder to crush. The FDA found that the changes had no effect on the most common way that the Purdue's pills were taken and abused: by swallowing them. 'The tamper-resistant properties will have no effect on abuse by the oral route (the most common mode of abuse).' Despite that warning, Purdue deceptively marketed its opioids in a manner falsely implying they stop abuse — and even prevent addiction.
context: Complaint describes how Purdue continued marketing an abuse-deterrent feature despite an FDA finding that it had no effect on the most common route of abuse.

label: Project Tango framing addiction as market opportunity
original_label: Project Tango framing addiction as market opportunity
quote: In September 2014, Kathe Sackler dialed in to a confidential call about Project Tango. Project Tango was a secret plan for Purdue to expand into the business of selling drugs to treat opioid addiction. In their internal documents, Kathe and staff wrote down what Purdue publicly denied for decades: that addictive opioids and opioid addiction are 'naturally linked.' They determined that Purdue should expand across 'the pain and addiction spectrum,' to become 'an end-to-end pain provider.' Purdue illustrated the end-to-end business model with a picture of a dark hole labeled 'Pain treatment' that a patient could fall into — and 'Opioid addiction treatment' waiting at the bottom.
context: Complaint describes how Purdue's leadership privately acknowledged the link between their opioids and addiction while planning to profit from both sides of the problem.

label: False press statements denying Sackler leadership role
original_label: False press statements denying Sackler leadership role
quote: In November, staff prepared statements to the press denying the Sacklers' involvement in Purdue. Their draft claimed: 'Sackler family members hold no leadership roles in the companies owned by the family trust.' That was a lie. Sackler family members held the controlling majority of seats on the Board and, in fact, controlled the company. A staff member reviewing the draft knew what was up and commented with apparent sarcasm: 'Love the ... statement.' Staff eventually told the press: 'Sackler family members hold no management positions.' Some employees worried about the deception. When journalists asked follow-up questions about the Sacklers, communications staff deliberated about whether to repeat the 'no management positions' claim. They double-checked that Purdue's top lawyers had ordered the statement. Then they arranged for one of the Sacklers' foreign companies to issue it, so U.S. employees would not be blamed: 'The statement will come out of Singapore.'
context: Complaint describes how Purdue issued false public denials of Sackler involvement, with deliberate efforts to obscure attribution and maintain the false narrative.

label: Board of Directors' failure to stop deceptive practices
original_label: Board of Directors' failure to stop deceptive practices
quote: Defendants Peter Boer, Judith Lewent, Cecil Pickett, Paulo Costa, and Ralph Snyderman took seats on the Board and knowingly advanced the Sacklers' scheme. They voted with the Sacklers on every single one of the hundreds of votes that came before them during their respective Board tenures. They voted with the Sacklers to hire hundreds more sales reps to carry out Purdue's unfair and deceptive sales tactics, including in Massachusetts. They voted with the Sacklers to implement incentive compensation policies that aggressively drove opioid sales, by placing outsized emphasis on prescription volume rather than compliance, including in Massachusetts.
context: Complaint describes board members as handlers/place managers who were positioned to control or stop the misconduct but failed to do so, instead voting consistently to advance it.

label: Sales VP Russell Gasdia pressured by Sacklers to increase sales
original_label: Sales VP Russell Gasdia pressured by Sacklers to increase sales
quote: The Sacklers' micromanagement was so intrusive that staff begged for relief. The VP of Sales and Marketing wrote to the CEO: 'Anything you can do to reduce the direct contact of Richard into the organization is appreciated.' When Richard Sackler wrote to managers, 'This is bad,' to criticize the sales of Purdue's Butrans opioid, the managers in turn drafted a warning for employees: 'Just today, Dr. Richard sent another email, 'This is bad,' referring to current Butrans trends. I am quite sure that Dr. Richard would not be sympathetic to the plight of the Boston District.' The manager then threatened to fire every sales rep in the Boston district.
context: Complaint describes how the Sacklers' direct pressure on executives created cascading pressure on field staff, with sales VP Gasdia unable to insulate operations from owner control.

label: Richard Sackler's field visits to supervise deceptive sales
original_label: Richard Sackler's field visits to supervise deceptive sales
quote: To make sure his orders were followed, Richard Sackler demanded to be sent into the field with the sales reps. Richard wanted a week shadowing Purdue sales reps, two reps per day. In horror, Gasdia appealed to Purdue's Chief Compliance Officer, warning that Richard Sackler promoting opioids was 'a potential compliance risk.' Compliance replied: 'LOL.' To make sure the Sacklers' involvement in marketing stayed secret, staff instructed: 'Richard needs to be mum and be anonymous.' About 5 last night, John [Stewart, the CEO] was walking by my office – I yelled out to stop him – and said that you had mentioned to me that Richard wanted to go into the field, and that you had raised concerns with me. John seemed angry, and asked if I had concerns. I told him could be issues and Richard could be out on a limb if he spoke about product at all or got into conversations with HCPs, or identified himself, especially with FDA Bad Ad possibilities. John agreed Richard would have to be mum throughout, and not identify himself other than as a home office person.
context: Complaint describes how Richard Sackler directly participated in field sales visits, with compliance officers and executives discussing how to conceal his involvement.

label: Compliance officer inadequacy in detecting fraud
original_label: Compliance officer inadequacy in detecting fraud
quote: Staff told the Sacklers that Purdue received 284 Reports of Concern about abuse and diversion of Purdue's opioids in Q4 2007, and they conducted only 21 field inquiries in response. Staff also reported to the Sacklers that they received 39 tips to Purdue's compliance hotline during the quarter, but Purdue did not report any of them to the authorities. In May, staff told the Sacklers that Purdue had violated its Corporate Integrity Agreement with the U.S. government by failing to supervise its sales reps. Because sales reps lobbying doctors poses a high risk of misconduct (no witnesses, and the rep is paid to increase opioid sales), the United States required that Purdue managers supervise sales reps in person at least 5 days each year. Purdue management disregarded that obligation and did not even set up a system to track it.
context: Complaint describes how Purdue's compliance apparatus received hundreds of reports but failed to conduct adequate investigations or escalate concerns to authorities.

label: CEO John Stewart's role in directing deceptive sales tactics
original_label: CEO John Stewart's role in directing deceptive sales tactics
quote: As CEO from 2007 to 2013, John Stewart headed up Purdue's unfair and deceptive campaign to get more Massachusetts residents to take more opioids at higher doses for longer periods of time. Stewart knowingly and intentionally sent sales reps to promote opioids in Massachusetts. At his direction, Purdue's sales reps visited Massachusetts prescribers more than 70,000 times. Stewart, in collaboration with sales executives like Russell Gasdia, recommended that Purdue increase the size of the sales force several times, more than doubling the number of sales reps during his tenure.
context: Complaint identifies CEO Stewart as a handler/place manager who was positioned to control sales operations and misconduct, but instead actively directed the deceptive campaign.

label: Massachusetts Attorney General investigation and lawsuit filing
original_label: Massachusetts Attorney General investigation and lawsuit filing
quote: On June 12, 2018, the Massachusetts Attorney General filed this suit to hold the Sacklers as well as Purdue accountable. Just as their employees predicted, the Sacklers tried to run. Richard Sackler was the first to go: he resigned from the Board in July. David Sackler quit in August. Theresa Sackler served her last day in September. As of the date of this filing, Ilene, Jonathan, Kathe, and Mortimer remain.
context: Complaint describes the filing of the lawsuit as a convergence break, where new external enforcement action caused the offenders to resign from positions of control.

label: Public health warnings and media coverage of opioid deaths
original_label: Public health warnings and media coverage of opioid deaths
quote: In April 2001, Massachusetts Attorney General investigated Purdue. In May 2001, the New York Times reported that 'OxyContin's sales have hit $1 billion, more than even Viagra's.' The same article noted that 'OxyContin has been a factor in the deaths of at least 120 people, and medical examiners are still counting.' When Time magazine published an article about OxyContin deaths in New England, Purdue employees told Richard Sackler they were concerned. Richard responded with a message to his staff. He wrote that Time's coverage of people who lost their lives to OxyContin was not 'balanced,' and the deaths were the fault of 'the drug addicts,' instead of Purdue.
context: Complaint describes media coverage of opioid-related deaths as a convergence break that increased scrutiny and affected Purdue's reputation, though the company attempted to counter the narrative.

label: New York Times reporting on Purdue's Region Zero list
original_label: New York Times reporting on Purdue's Region Zero list
quote: In 2012, the Los Angeles Times had studied coroner's records and revealed that overdoses killed thousands of patients who were taking opioids prescribed by their doctors, refuting the Sacklers' lie that patients who are prescribed opioids don't get addicted and die. The next year, the Los Angeles Times revealed that Purdue tracked illegal sales of OxyContin with a secret list of 1,800 doctors code-named Region Zero, but did not report them to the authorities. The 'mitigation effort' that the Sacklers ordered was not designed to protect patients from overdoses or from illegal prescribers, but instead to protect the Sacklers from reporters revealing the truth.
context: Complaint describes journalism investigating Purdue's deceptive practices and hidden tracking of suspicious prescribers as a convergence break, with Purdue attempting to manage the narrative.

label: CDC opioid prescribing guidelines warning against high doses
original_label: CDC opioid prescribing guidelines warning against high doses
quote: In April, the Sacklers considered exactly how much money was riding on their strategy of pushing higher doses of opioids. The month before, the U.S. Centers for Disease Control announced guidelines to try to slow the epidemic of opioid overdose and death. The CDC urged prescribers to avoid doses higher than 30mg of Purdue's OxyContin twice per day. The CDC discouraged twice-a-day prescriptions of all three of Purdue's most profitable strengths — 40mg, 60mg, and 80mg. Staff studied how much money Purdue was making from its high dose strategy and told the Sacklers that $23,964,122 was at risk in Massachusetts each year.
context: Complaint describes CDC guidance issuing recommendations contrary to Purdue's business model, creating a convergence break where external health authorities began restricting opioid prescribing.

label: New Yorker article revealing Sackler family involvement
original_label: New Yorker article revealing Sackler family involvement
quote: On October 17, Beverly Sackler served her last day on the Board. It was the beginning of the end for the Sackler family. A week later, the New Yorker published an article entitled 'The Family That Built an Empire of Pain.' The story quoted a former FDA Commissioner: 'the goal should have been to sell the least dose of the drug to the smallest number of patients.' The reporter concluded: 'Purdue set out to do exactly the opposite.'
context: Complaint describes a major media investigation that directly named the Sackler family's responsibility for the opioid crisis, coinciding with Beverly Sackler's departure from the board.

label: CEO directs sales strategy and opioid volume targets
original_label: CEO directs sales strategy and opioid volume targets
quote: In January 2014, just a few months before Massachusetts declared the opioid epidemic a public health emergency, Timney picked up as CEO where John Stewart left off, directing and overseeing the sale and marketing of Purdue's opioids and the expansion of the sales force, including in Massachusetts. Timney directed Purdue sales reps to target Massachusetts doctors to prescribe opioids to more patients, at higher doses, for longer periods of time.
context: Complaint allegations against Mark Timney as CEO, describing his authority to direct sales operations and strategy.

label: Sales VP controls sales strategy and rep compensation
original_label: Sales VP controls sales strategy and rep compensation
quote: Russell Gasdia worked at the heart of Purdue's deceptive sales campaign. From 2007 until 2014, Gasdia was Purdue's Vice President of Sales and Marketing. He was responsible for getting more patients on opioids, at higher doses, for longer periods of time. By breaking the law, he enjoyed the privileges of life as a top Purdue executive, and he exposed families across Massachusetts to addiction, overdose, and death.
context: Complaint allegations identifying Gasdia's position and authority over the sales campaign.

label: Chief Medical Officer develops sales materials and instructs reps
original_label: Chief Medical Officer develops sales materials and instructs reps
quote: In each of his positions, Landau worked to get more Massachusetts patients on opioids at higher doses for longer periods of time. As Chief Medical Officer, he helped to develop the sales strategy and materials and instruct reps in how to sell Purdue's drugs. As CEO, he oversaw the whole sales scheme.
context: Complaint allegations describing Landau's roles and responsibilities across positions.

label: Sackler family controls company through board positions
original_label: Sackler family controls company through board positions
quote: To convince the Sacklers to make him CEO, Landau wrote a plan that he titled: 'SACKLER PHARMA ENTERPRISE.' He started by admitting that the Sacklers in fact controlled the company like chief executive officers. The family ran 'the global Sackler pharmaceutical enterprise … with the Board of Directors serving as the 'de-facto' CEO.'
context: Landau's internal memo to the Sacklers describing their ultimate control of Purdue operations.

label: Doctors with high opioid prescribing volume as targets
original_label: Doctors with high opioid prescribing volume as targets
quote: Gasdia had his hands on every part of Purdue's deceptive sales campaign: from the fundamentals of getting more patients on opioids at higher doses for longer periods; to the targeting of prolific opioid prescribers; to paying doctors to promote Purdue opioids; to concealing Purdue's list of problem doctors codenamed Region Zero; to deciding what would get a sales rep hired or fired.
context: Complaint describing Gasdia's strategy of targeting prolific prescribers as vulnerable to intensified promotion.

label: Doctors under investigation targeted for sales visits
original_label: Doctors under investigation targeted for sales visits
quote: In 2002, staff sent Gasdia an email identifying four Massachusetts OxyContin prescribers believed to be the subjects of a federal investigation. The urgency of the message was explicit: 'This is most urgent.' Gasdia did not steer Purdue reps away from the doctors. Instead, he did the opposite and ordered reps to focus on them as highly-profitable 'Super Core' targets. Under Gasdia's direction, sales reps visited those specific doctors hundreds of times.
context: Email from staff to Gasdia flagging targeted doctors under investigation; Gasdia's response to intensify sales calls.

label: Doctor with disciplinary history paid to promote opioids
original_label: Doctor with disciplinary history paid to promote opioids
quote: Weeks earlier, Jacobs had admitted in disciplinary proceedings before the Massachusetts Board of Registration in Medicine that he continuously prescribed narcotics to patients, ignored the risk of addiction, and kept prescribing narcotics even after his patients overdosed. But Purdue's data showed that Jacobs was a top prescriber of Purdue opioids. So Purdue paid him to encourage other doctors to prescribe Purdue's drugs.
context: Complaint describing Purdue's strategy of recruiting a doctor with known prescribing abuses as a paid speaker.

label: Restricted-access prescribers targeted through call center workaround
original_label: Restricted-access prescribers targeted through call center workaround
quote: When some health care systems stopped allowing sales reps to visit doctor's offices, Timney developed a work-around. Under his direction, Purdue created a call center where sales reps telephoned doctors and hospitals, including facilities with 'no-see' policies, to encourage them to prescribe more opioids.
context: Complaint describing Timney's response to access restrictions by creating alternative promotion channels.

label: Patients vulnerable to long-term opioid use remain attractive market
original_label: Patients vulnerable to long-term opioid use remain attractive market
quote: Gasdia also led Purdue's efforts to increase profit by keeping patients on opioids for longer periods of time. In 2012, Gasdia and his staff studied Purdue's confidential data on 'length of therapy' and developed sales tactics to extend it. They prepared a presentation for the Board on this strategy, reporting that, because of Purdue's marketing: 'More patients remain on therapy at 90 days' and 'Patients remain on therapy 41 days longer.'
context: Board presentation to Gasdia showing measurement and targeting of patients' length of therapy as profit driver.

label: FDA required monitoring system after 2007 conviction
original_label: FDA required monitoring system after 2007 conviction
quote: The 2007 Judgment required Purdue to establish an Abuse and Diversion Detection and Reporting System. The judgment also provided that when Purdue learned of improper prescribing by its target doctors, it must terminate the sales rep's visits and notify the authorities.
context: Court judgment as external mandate for internal abuse detection post-2007.

label: Abuse detection system inadequate despite mandatory requirement
original_label: Abuse detection system inadequate despite mandatory requirement
quote: Later that month, Timney gave an internal presentation demonstrating the inadequacies of Purdue's 'system' for tracking prescribers that were prescribing opioids inappropriately. The presentation made clear that as late as 2016, Purdue's Abuse and Diversion Detection system consisted of ad hoc, manual reviews of sales reps' call notes, media reports, internet searches, and prescribing records to identify opioid abuse and adverse events. Purdue had no system capable of providing meaningful deterrence, a full nine years after the 2007 convictions and settlement required one.
context: Internal presentation by Timney showing the absence of effective monitoring despite court mandate.

label: Regulatory mandate for system delegated to company itself
original_label: Regulatory mandate for system delegated to company itself
quote: The judgment required that Purdue implement an Abuse and Diversion Detection and Reporting System that operated continuously and generated reports at least quarterly. But Purdue could design the system itself. In July 2011, Purdue submitted its self-designed system for the court's consideration.
context: Complaint describing delegation of oversight design to Purdue itself after conviction.

label: Sales reps avoid email to evade discovery
original_label: Sales reps avoid email to evade discovery
quote: Purdue's most severe policy against email prohibited sales reps from writing down in emails their sales pitches to doctors. By insisting that sales reps discuss opioids only in face-to-face oral conversations, Purdue tried to avoid discoverable evidence of its misconduct. As the top sales and marketing executive in the company, Gasdia personally enforced that rule with a vengeance. When Gasdia learned that a sales rep had sent a doctor email about Purdue opioids, he ordered: 'Fire her now! We can't afford this.'
context: Complaint describing Purdue's deliberate use of oral-only communication to evade discovery routines.

label: Company avoids email after notification of investigation
original_label: Company avoids email after notification of investigation
quote: The defendants' unfair and deceptive conduct was well concealed. The defendants deliberately conducted much of their deception through in-person sales visits, in order to avoid a potentially discoverable paper trail. Purdue prohibited its sales reps from emailing doctors. After this Office notified Purdue of our investigation, Purdue changed its decade-old procedure so that sales reps would not write down descriptions of their conversations with doctors for every sales visit, even in Purdue's internal records.
context: Attorney General's allegation that Purdue modified documentation practices after investigation notification.

label: Document destruction ordered to limit evidence trail
original_label: Document destruction ordered to limit evidence trail
quote: When staff emailed Gasdia a detailed report of illegal OxyContin trafficking, he responded: 'These should not be on email. Tell [District Managers] and Reps to use fax.' When the Northeast Regional Manager emailed Gasdia about the arrest of a profitable 'core physician' in Massachusetts, Gasdia ordered: 'Discontinue use of email on this subject.'
